books.title: Dogs at Work
books.art_why: Working dogs, people, and modern jobs are real-world subjects best shown in photographs.

pages.text: Dogs at Work or or at at.
pages.brief: Several dogs of different breeds are shown together at work, each dog representing a different kind of job. The dogs stand and sit in a clear, simple scene that introduces the many ways dogs can work.

pages.text: or at at.
pages.brief: A very sparse, quiet page with soft color and open space, placed before the introduction. The page has almost no picture content, creating a calm pause before the book begins with dogs at work and the many jobs they can do.

pages.text: Introduction You probably know that some dogs aren’t just pets—they hold jobs! Some dogs can work on farms, guarding or herding animals. Other dogs can pull sleds or help people hunt. Dogs have worked with people for thousands of years. What makes dogs such great workers? They learn fast, and they can also hear and smell better than we can. This means that dogs can do jobs that people can’t. Some of their jobs may surprise you.
pages.brief: A group of working dogs is shown in different settings: one dog on a farm guarding or herding animals, another pulling a sled, and another helping a person hunt. The dogs look alert, showing how fast they learn and how they use hearing and smell.

pages.text: Service and Therapy Dogs Many dogs work with people to help them feel better. These dogs are called therapy dogs. Therapy dogs comfort people and keep them calm. These dogs sometimes visit sick people in hospitals to cheer them up. Therapy dogs need to have a friendly personality. They are trained to react calmly to new places, smells, and people.
pages.brief: A friendly therapy dog stands calmly beside a sick person in a hospital, letting the person pet it. The dog looks relaxed and gentle in the new hospital room, showing the calm, friendly personality therapy dogs need when they visit people to cheer them up.

pages.text: Other dogs help people with disabilities. These dogs are called service dogs. Service dogs can do many different jobs. For example, guide dogs help people who cannot see well. These dogs are trained to keep people from stepping into traffic. Guide dogs are also trained to lead their owner around objects. That way, their owner won’t trip or fall. Tennille the Guide Dog Guide dogs can be trained to help their owner have adventures. A guide dog named Tennille helped her owner hike in the wilderness. Tennille was the first guide dog trained to do this. Her owner, Trevor Thomas, is blind. Tennille helped Thomas over and around large rocks. She also looked for trail signs and led Thomas up to them. Thomas would then read the signs with his fingers. Thomas hopes that he and Tennille can encourage other blind people to follow their example.
pages.brief: A guide dog named Tennille leads her blind owner, Trevor Thomas, along a wilderness trail. She helps him over and around large rocks, then leads him to a trail sign so he can read it with his fingers. The scene shows their adventure together.

pages.text: Some service dogs help people who can’t hear well. These dogs listen for noises (like a doorbell), touch their owner, and move toward the noise. Some service dogs also help their owner move around. They pull wheelchairs, pick up dropped objects, press buttons, and open doors.
pages.brief: A service dog touches its owner to alert them to a noise, then moves toward a doorbell. Nearby, another service dog pulls a wheelchair, picks up a dropped object, presses a button, and opens a door, showing the different ways service dogs help people hear and move around.

pages.text: Some service dogs use their nose to help their owner. For example, dogs can help people with low blood sugar. These dogs can smell changes in blood and alert their owner to eat food or take medicine. Other service dogs can smell when a person is about to have a seizure. These sudden attacks cause body spasms and other problems. Service dogs can warn the person before it happens. Other dogs work with children who have food allergies. Some children can’t eat peanuts. Service dogs can help them by smelling hidden peanuts in food.
pages.brief: A service dog sniffs near its owner and alerts them by nudging, as the owner reaches for food or medicine. In another part of the scene, a dog sits beside a child with food allergies, sniffing for hidden peanuts in food to warn the child.

pages.text: Search-and-Rescue Dogs Some dogs work to find people who are lost, hurt, or trapped. These dogs are called search-and-rescue (SAR) dogs. Many SAR dogs use their powerful nose to find people who need help. Dogs can be trained to do this in two different ways. The first way is through “tracking”— putting their nose to the ground to follow a scent. Tracking dogs can follow a missing person when the scent is fresh. They need to work quickly, before the scent fades.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog puts its nose to the ground and follows a scent, tracking a missing person. The dog works quickly before the scent fades, using its powerful nose to find someone who is lost, hurt, or trapped.

pages.text: The second way that dogs can search for missing people is by sniffing the air instead of the ground. These “air-scent” dogs often work in a big search area. Using only their nose, they can find skiers trapped under 5 meters (16 ft.) of snow. They can also find lost hikers. They can even find people trapped in buildings that have fallen down.
pages.brief: An air-scent dog stands in a wide search area with its nose lifted to sniff the air. The dog searches for lost hikers, skiers trapped under deep snow, and people trapped in fallen buildings, using only its nose to find them.

pages.text: Other SAR dogs work in the water instead of on land. Water rescue dogs can be trained to pull drowning people to safety. They can find people underwater and pull small boats to land. Water rescue dogs need to be strong swimmers. For this reason, big dogs like Newfoundlands make good water rescue dogs. Newfoundland dogs have waterproof fur and webbed toes, and they love to swim. They are also much stronger than human lifeguards. A 68-kilogram (150 lb.) Newfoundland can pull ten people to safety at once!
pages.brief: A large Newfoundland water rescue dog swims strongly in the water, pulling a drowning person to safety. The dog has waterproof fur and webbed toes, and it can also find people underwater and pull a small boat to land.

pages.text: Detection Dogs Some dogs work as detectives. These dogs are called detection dogs. They use their sense of smell to help people find things that are hidden. Police use detection dogs often. They use arson dogs when a building has burned down. It may be hard to find out whether someone started the fire on purpose. Arson dogs sniff for chemicals that might have been used to start the fire.
pages.brief: A detection dog, an arson dog, sniffs through the burned ruins of a building. The dog works with police to find chemicals that might have been used to start the fire on purpose, using its sense of smell to find hidden evidence.

pages.text: Detection dogs are also used at airports and border crossings. These dogs search for objects that cannot be brought into a country or onto a plane. It’s usually illegal to bring fresh fruit or live animals across a border without permission. Detection dogs can find these things hidden in people’s bags. Police also use detection dogs to find criminals. Other detection dogs work outside the world of crime. For example, some dogs are trained to search for termites in houses and other buildings. Termites damage buildings by eating wood. They are hard for humans to find, but termite dogs can sniff them out.
pages.brief: At an airport or border crossing, a detection dog sniffs people’s bags for hidden fresh fruit or live animals. In another setting, a termite dog searches a house or building for termites that damage wood, while police also use detection dogs to find criminals.

pages.text: Detection dogs may even be able to help doctors in the future. Some dogs, for example, seem to be able to smell cancer in humans. Scientists are studying these dogs to see if they can help doctors find cancer quickly in their patients. Odd Jobs Dogs quickly learn to do even unusual jobs. For example, a dog named Piper worked with his owner at an airport in Michigan. His job was to chase wild birds out of the path of planes on runways. Another group of dogs had an unusual job at an oceanside baseball park in San Francisco. These dogs jumped into the ocean to get balls that were hit into the water. The program is now over, but for a time, baseball fans loved to collect these “Splash Hit” balls.
pages.brief: A dog named Piper chases wild birds off an airport runway in Michigan, clearing the path of planes. At an oceanside baseball park in San Francisco, dogs jump into the ocean to fetch balls hit into the water, while baseball fans collect the balls; that program is now over.

pages.text: Conclusion Dogs help us do many types of jobs. As our work changes and grows, so do the jobs we give to dogs. From sniffing out cancer cells to pulling a swimmer to safety, dogs help humans in many ways. Their strength, friendliness, intelligence, and powerful senses make dogs wonderful workers.
pages.brief: A montage of working dogs shows one dog sniffing for cancer cells and another pulling a swimmer to safety. Around them are dogs using their strength, friendliness, intelligence, and powerful senses to help humans in many different jobs.

books.title: Extreme Animals
books.art_why: The book is about real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Many unusual animals have special stories to tell. They seem to go to extremes to get noticed. Something about each of these animals makes them different from other types of animals. It might be an ability, or a special talent, that makes them stand out. Is it their speed or their size—or even their coloration? One is as tall as a two-story house, and another is as small as a mouse. Maybe one can jump higher or hide in a small space; or they can see farther or scream louder. This book tells many odd, unknown, and fun facts about these unusual animals, and what makes them different and special. Read on to learn about some of the most extreme animals in the world.
pages.brief: A varied group of unusual animals appears together: one enormous animal stands as tall as a two-story house, while a tiny animal is as small as a mouse. Others are shown jumping high, hiding in a small space, looking into the distance, and calling loudly, each with a different color or shape.

pages.text: Biggest A giant blue whale is as long as half of a football field. It is the largest mammal to inhabit the Earth—now or ever. Its body is so heavy that it has to be supported by water. If it were a land animal instead, a blue whale would be crushed by its own weight. A baby elephant can weigh 136 kilograms (300 lbs) when it’s born, and it will keep growing for thirty years. An average-sized adult elephant weighs as much as two pickup trucks, but some extra-large elephants have weighed twice as much. A grown male can reach a height of over fifteen feet. An adult giraffe is as tall as a two-story house. Its long, powerful neck and long legs make it the tallest land animal anywhere. A baby giraffe is already 1.8 meters (6 ft) tall when it’s born.
pages.brief: A giant blue whale floats in the ocean, its huge body held up by the water. On land, a baby elephant stands beside a much larger adult elephant. Nearby, an adult giraffe reaches the height of a two-story house, with a long neck and long legs.

pages.text: Smallest A little Chihuahua looks as if it’s all ears! This friendly little dog is so small that it can fit into your pocket and go along with you wherever you go. It has a sweet temperament, but it’s very brave and will bark at dogs that are many times its tiny size.
pages.brief: A tiny Chihuahua with very large ears stands bravely near a pocket. The little dog has a sweet expression but barks boldly at dogs many times its size. Its small body looks as if it could fit into a pocket and travel along wherever a person goes.

pages.text: Loudest A blue whale’s cry, or song, is as loud as the noise of a rocket being launched. It will sing for as long as ten hours— and its sound can be heard far away in the ocean. Quietest A tall, long-legged giraffe is one of the quietest animals. It isn’t quiet because it’s shy—it just doesn’t use its voice. Instead of sounds, a giraffe communicates with body language.
pages.brief: In the ocean, a blue whale sings with its mouth open, its call as powerful as a rocket launch. Far away, a tall giraffe stands quietly on open ground, using only body language instead of sound. The whale is underwater; the giraffe is long-legged and silent.

pages.text: Longest Life The big, slow, tortoise that lives in the Galapagos Islands has a lot of time to explore its island home from one end to the other—as it can live for 150 to 200 years. Shortest Life A mayfly usually lives only one day after it hatches into an adult insect. It has a lot to do during its short life, including finding a mate, so it doesn’t even stop to eat or drink! Slowest Snails don’t hurry for any reason. You could take a nap or read a story while a garden snail slowly crawls across your shoe.
pages.brief: On the Galapagos Islands, a big, slow tortoise crawls across rocky ground, taking its time. Nearby, an adult mayfly flies through the air during its single day of life. A garden snail creeps slowly across a shoe, moving without any hurry.

pages.text: Fastest An adult ostrich can run as fast as a racehorse. The tall, long-legged ostrich may look awkward when it walks, but it’s the fastest land animal on two feet.
pages.brief: An adult ostrich sprints across open ground on two long legs. Its tall body looks awkward as it runs, but it moves as fast as a racehorse. The ostrich's long neck is stretched forward, and its strong legs carry it swiftly over the land.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Reptiles Snakes have very sharp vision, but they never shut their eyes—even when they sleep. Snakes have transparent eyelids that slide down to protect their open eyes from dust.
pages.brief: A snake rests in a dry, dusty place with its eyes wide open. Transparent eyelids slide down over the open eyes to protect them from dust, so the snake never shuts its eyes, even while it sleeps. Its sharp gaze stays fixed ahead.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Water Creatures No licking! The tongue of a big humpback whale weighs as much as a small car does.
pages.brief: A huge humpback whale swims in the ocean with its mouth open, showing its enormous tongue. The tongue is so big and heavy that it weighs as much as a small car. Water surrounds the whale as it moves through the sea.

pages.text: A mudskipper is an athletic fish that can climb a tree. Even though it’s a fish, it can move faster on land than it can swim in the water. The flat, diamond-shaped halibut is the largest flatfish. It looks odd to us because both of its eyes are located on the same side of its head. Fun Facts About Mammals Every zebra has its own pattern of stripes so each zebra is slightly different. Most zebras may look alike to us—but not to other zebras.
pages.brief: A mudskipper fish climbs a tree trunk above the water, its body braced for movement. On the seafloor, a flat, diamond-shaped halibut rests with both eyes on the same side of its head. Nearby, a zebra stands with its own unique pattern of stripes.

pages.text: A kangaroo can lean back and balance on its big tail while punching and kicking with all four feet at the same time. A big, awkward- looking hippopotamus can run faster than a person. For a short distance, a hippo can run 48 to 64 kilometers per hour (30-40 mph). A camel can close its nose to keep out the blowing desert sand. It can also cool the air that it breathes in just by twitching its nose.
pages.brief: A kangaroo leans back on its big tail, balancing while it punches and kicks with all four feet. A heavy-looking hippopotamus runs fast over the ground. In blowing desert sand, a camel closes its nose to keep the sand out while it breathes.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Insects A butterfly stands on its food. It has little taste bud sensors in its feet that tell it whether it’s standing on something good to eat.
pages.brief: A butterfly stands on its food, its feet touching the surface beneath it. Tiny taste sensors in its feet tell it whether the food is good to eat. The butterfly's wings are still as it balances on the meal.

pages.text: Fun Facts About Birds An eagle is a very large bird, but it weighs very little. Its bones are hollow to help it fly at high altitudes without tiring. Its bones are so lightweight that its feathers actually weigh more than its bones do.
pages.brief: A large eagle soars high in the sky with its broad wings spread. Its body is very light because its bones are hollow, helping it fly without tiring. Its feathers are thick and prominent, weighing more than its lightweight bones.

pages.text: What other extreme animals do you know?
pages.brief: A wide natural scene brings together several extreme animals: a blue whale in the ocean, a tall giraffe, a running ostrich, a kangaroo balanced on its tail, and an eagle overhead. The group fills the view, inviting the viewer to think of more.

books.title: All About Kites
books.art_why: Modern kites, ships, tools, and real places can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Few things are as bright and lively as a sky filled with colorful, dancing kites! Each kite seems to be competing for attention. Long- tailed dragons, spinning stars, and favorite cartoon characters are all flying high. Kites are no longer just simple toys. Modern materials and engineering methods have changed kites. New kites are bigger, lighter, and stronger. Many kites these days move like acrobats in the sky.
pages.brief: A wide, bright sky is filled with colorful kites dancing and competing for attention: a long-tailed dragon, a spinning star, and a favorite cartoon character fly high. The modern kites look bigger, lighter, and stronger, moving like acrobats above the ground.

pages.text: History of Kites Thousands of years ago, the first toy kites were named after the kite bird. This large, graceful bird has a very wide wingspan. Many early kites were shaped like birds, but people kept experimenting with ways to make kites. Slowly, kites became more elaborate. They took on certain features and flight patterns. There are very early records of kite flying in Chinese history. The first written story of kite flying is over 2,200 years old. According to this story, the Chinese General Han Hsin had to figure out how far to tunnel under his enemy’s walls. He used a kite to measure the distance. Chinese legends also describe the thinkers Mozi and Lu Ban creating a kite that lifted Lu Ban into the air.
pages.brief: A large kite bird with a very wide wingspan flies above early bird-shaped kites. In a Chinese scene, General Han Hsin uses a kite to measure distance near enemy walls, while the thinkers Mozi and Lu Ban work with an early kite that lifts Lu Ban into the air.

pages.text: Some kites have made history. The famous American diplomat and inventor Ben Franklin loved testing ideas. He used a kite to prove his idea that lightning was made of electric current. On a stormy day, he and his son tied a metal key to a kite string. They flew their kite high into the storm clouds. Just as Franklin expected, electricity from the clouds ran down the wet string to the metal key. When he reached toward the key, the electricity jumped from the key and gave him a shock! Warning: Don’t try this experiment! When Franklin tried it again, he was hurt badly.
pages.brief: On a stormy day, Ben Franklin and his son fly a kite high into dark storm clouds. A metal key is tied to the wet kite string. Electricity runs down the string to the key, and a spark jumps toward Franklin’s reaching hand.

pages.text: Unusual Uses for Kites Fishing: Fish like to chase things in the water. Some people want to reach fish that swim far from shore. They tie a shiny fishhook with bait to the long tail of a kite. The kite skips the bait through the water. The fish see it, bite it, and are caught and reeled in. Weather charts: For years, scientists used a special box kite to carry weather instruments up in the air. They used the kite to chart and record wind speeds and air temperatures.
pages.brief: Near the shore, a shiny fishhook with bait is tied to a long kite tail and skipped through the water so fish chase and bite it. Nearby, scientists raise a special box kite carrying weather instruments to chart wind speeds and air temperatures high above.

pages.text: Real wind power: Long-distance cargo ships burn large amounts of fuel. They also pollute the air. One German shipping company is using special kites to help reduce both problems. The big kite helps pull the ship so the ship’s engines will burn less fuel every day. As they burn less fuel, less air pollution will be produced.
pages.brief: A long-distance cargo ship crosses the water while a big special kite pulls it forward. The German shipping company’s kite helps the ship’s engines burn less fuel each day, reducing air pollution from the ship’s long journey.

pages.text: Not all spies are well-trained human snoops. For years, armies fastened small, powerful cameras to kites to fly over and spy on enemy locations. Armies have also used kites for shooting practice. These special kites could twist, dive, and avoid bullets like military fighter planes.
pages.brief: Small, powerful cameras are fastened to kites flying over enemy locations to spy for armies. Other special kites twist, dive, and avoid bullets during shooting practice, moving like military fighter planes above the training area.

pages.text: Watching a kite sail lightly through the sky still makes everyone smile. With a little practice, almost anyone can put a kite together and learn to fly it. One day, you may want to test your new kite skills on stunt kites with two or more strings. Or you may want to try a sport such as kitesurfing. In this sport, a big power kite pulls your surfboard!
pages.brief: People watch a kite sail lightly through the sky and smile. With practice, almost anyone can put a kite together and fly it. Stunt kites with two or more strings move overhead, and a big power kite pulls a kitesurfer’s surfboard across the water.

pages.text: Make Your Own Kite You’ll need: • two lightweight, smooth sticks, one 3 feet (90 cm) long, the other 2 feet (60 cm) • a large plastic trash bag, cut open • a long strip of lightweight cloth or plastic for the tail • strong tape Step 1: Form a cross shape with the sticks. Wrap tape around the sticks where they meet.
pages.brief: Two lightweight, smooth sticks, one three feet long and one two feet long, lie beside an opened plastic trash bag, a long lightweight tail strip, and strong tape. The sticks form a cross shape, with tape wrapped around the place where they meet.

pages.text: Step 2: Cut off a 4-foot (120 cm) piece of string. Tape each end of the string to each end of the long stick. This string is called the bridle. Tie one end of the rest of the string to the middle of the bridle. Step 3: Lay the cross on the open plastic bag. Cut a diamond shape around it. Make sure to cut the diamond shape wider than the ends of the sticks.
pages.brief: A four-foot piece of string is taped from one end of the long stick to the other, making a bridle. The rest of the string ties to the middle of the bridle. The cross lies on the opened plastic bag, and a diamond shape is cut wider than the stick ends.

pages.text: Step 4: Fold the corners of the diamond over the ends of the sticks. Tape the corners tightly to the sticks. Step 5: For a tail, tape the strip of cloth or plastic to the bottom of the kite. Kite Safety • Remember to choose an open, safe place to fly your kite. • Don’t fly your kite near power lines. Keep away from trees, roads, and airports. • Don’t fly a kite in the rain or when you hear thunder. • Be sure nothing is on the ground to trip over.
pages.brief: The diamond’s corners are folded over the stick ends and taped tightly. A lightweight tail strip is taped to the kite’s bottom. The finished kite is shown with an open, safe flying place away from power lines, trees, roads, airports, rain, thunder, and things on the ground to trip over.

pages.text: When it’s time to test your first kite, pick a breezy day. Take your kite to a flat, open area. You can even go to a beach if one is nearby. Look around you to be sure there are no power lines or big trees to tangle your kite. Make sure there is nothing on the ground you could trip over. Ready to start? Hold your kite up by the bridle and run into the wind. When you feel it tug, let go of the kite! Let out a little string, slowly, until you feel the wind pulling your kite. Keep letting out more string until your kite is flying high!
pages.brief: On a breezy day in a flat, open area or nearby beach, a person holds the kite up by the bridle and runs into the wind. When the kite tugs, the person lets go and slowly lets out string until the kite flies high, away from power lines and big trees.

books.title: Coral Reefs
books.art_why: Coral reefs are real, present-day ocean habitats that can be photographed.

pages.text: Coral Reefs.
pages.brief: A wide underwater view of a coral reef fills the scene, with branching and rounded corals in pink, orange, and green, small fish swimming between them, and bright sunlight filtering down from above through clear tropical water.

pages.text: Introduction Earth’s tropical oceans contain places of wonder and beauty known as coral reefs. These huge undersea communities are home to thousands of living things. Day and night, animals hunt, eat, and avoid being eaten. They depend on each other for food, shelter, and safety. Almost one-fourth of all ocean plants and animals live around coral reefs. Fish, sea turtles, sea stars, and many other animals make reefs their home. Visitors include seabirds and dolphins.
pages.brief: A tropical coral reef underwater community teems with fish, a sea turtle, sea stars, and many small animals; seabirds fly above the surface and dolphins swim nearby as animals hunt, eat, and avoid being eaten.

pages.text: What Is Coral? At first glance, coral may look like oddly shaped rocks or plants. In fact, corals are tiny animals called polyps (PAH-lips). Most polyps are smaller than a pea. One branch or mound of coral can have thousands of polyps. Each polyp has a tubelike body and a mouth with tiny tentacles. Polyps are eating machines. At night, they open their tentacles to catch tiny animals. Hundreds of kinds of corals live in the ocean. Most are one of two kinds. Hard corals, also known as stony corals, form hard skeletons. Over time, many millions of these hard skeletons build up and form reefs.
pages.brief: A close-up view of coral polyps smaller than peas, each with a tubelike body and a mouth with tiny tentacles; at night the tentacles open to catch tiny animals, while hard stony coral skeletons build into a reef.

pages.text: Most stony corals live together with algae (AL-jee). Algae are simple cousins of plants. They supply food for the corals and for many reef fish. Soft corals can bend with the currents. They often look like trees, bushes, or other plants. Algae live in the bodies of some, but not all, soft corals.
pages.brief: Stony corals live together with algae on a sunlit reef, while soft corals bend with the currents and look like trees, bushes, or other plants; algae supply food for corals and many reef fish around them.

pages.text: A Busy Underwater Community Most people think of brightly colored fish when they think about coral reefs—and with good reason. Thousands of kinds of fish live on reefs. The reefs provide them with food. Reefs also protect them from animals that hunt them for food. Shrimp, lobsters, and crabs also find food at reefs. Sea stars catch small animals that hide among the coral branches. Sea anemones, which look like flowers, wait for their next meal to drift past.
pages.brief: A busy reef scene shows brightly colored fish swimming among coral, shrimp, lobsters, and crabs finding food, a sea star catching small animals hidden in coral branches, and sea anemones that look like flowers waiting as meals drift past.

pages.text: Coral reefs support thousands of kinds of living things. They are important in other ways, too. Reefs help protect coasts from storms and floods. By keeping soil in place, they protect coasts from erosion. Coral reefs also feed and shelter animals that provide much of the world’s seafood. They help many countries bring in money and have food to eat. Also, reef plants and animals are used in medicines. Medicines from Coral Reefs Scientists have made medicines from living things on coral reefs, and more are likely on the way. Corals produce something that is used to treat asthma and arthritis. Medicines that treat several different kinds of cancer come from coral reefs, too. Scientists are also studying reef animals for ways to treat infections and skin problems.
pages.brief: A coastal coral reef softens storm waves and holds soil in place near the shore, while fish and seafood animals find food and shelter; scientists in a lab study reef corals and animals to make medicines for asthma, arthritis, cancer, infections, and skin problems.

pages.text: The Coral Reef Zone Where Are Coral Reefs? Most reefs are close to shore in warm tropical waters. They also form where warm currents flow from the tropics, such as in Florida. Coral grows best in warm water that is between 21 and 29 degrees Celsius (70–84°F). Since algae need sunlight to make food, most corals live near the water’s surface. There are three kinds of coral reefs. Fringing reefs are close to shore. They usually follow the natural shoreline, or fringe, of the land. Barrier reefs have a large, deep area of water between them and the shore. The world’s largest barrier reef is the Great Barrier Reef in Australia. It is 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long.
pages.brief: Warm, shallow tropical water near shore and around Florida supports sunlit coral reefs; a fringing reef follows the shoreline, a barrier reef lies across deep water, and Australia's Great Barrier Reef stretches 2,300 kilometers long.

pages.text: The Great Barrier Reef is made up of over three thousand different reefs and islands. It is home to nearly two thousand kinds of fish. Atolls are the third type of reef. They’re shaped like circles. They form around the outside of an old sinking island or island volcano. Over time, the island sinks or the volcano breaks apart. Then a small body of water called a lagoon forms in the center.
pages.brief: The Great Barrier Reef holds over three thousand reefs and islands and nearly two thousand kinds of fish; nearby, a circular atoll surrounds an old sinking island or island volcano, with a small lagoon forming in its center.

pages.text: Dangers to Coral Reefs Coral reefs are fragile, and many things can damage them. Large, powerful tsunami (soo-NAH-mee) waves can break reefs. Most damage is caused by people, however. Many scientists think that pollution is partly to blame for coral diseases. These diseases can wipe out a coral reef in weeks. Warmer ocean water due to global warming also plays a part.
pages.brief: Powerful tsunami waves break across a fragile coral reef, while polluted water spreads over corals affected by disease that can wipe out a reef in weeks; people's activities and warmer ocean water are shown as the main dangers.

pages.text: Global Warming Global warming is a rise in the average temperature of Earth’s air and oceans large enough to change long-term weather patterns. Global warming today is mostly caused by human activities. These include clearing land for farming and burning coal, oil, and gas. These things make large amounts of carbon dioxide gas. This gas enters the air around Earth and traps heat close to Earth’s surface. Global warming is causing many problems. They include more bad storms and dangers to natural communities. Scientists expect the problems to get worse unless we cut way back on the activities that make so much carbon dioxide. Another problem is known as bleaching. It also results from ocean water getting too warm. When this happens, the algae in coral polyps change in a way that harms the polyps. To stay safe, the polyps get rid of the algae. Since the polyps get most of their food from algae, they begin to starve. They also lose their color, which makes them look bleached.
pages.brief: A landscape shows cleared farmland and smokestacks burning coal, oil, and gas, sending carbon dioxide into the air and trapping heat near Earth's surface; below, warming ocean water harms algae inside coral polyps, which expel the algae, starve, and turn pale.

pages.text: Corals can sometimes recover from bleaching. But if the cause of bleaching continues, both the corals and the reef will die. Bleaching now affects three-fourths of coral reefs. Because of human activities, Earth’s oceans also contain too much carbon dioxide. The extra carbon dioxide makes ocean water more acidic. As a result, corals can’t take in a certain chemical that keeps their skeletons healthy. Without it, their skeletons dissolve. People are harming coral reefs in other ways, too. Fishing methods that use poisons and explosives have destroyed over half the reefs in the Philippines. Building along coasts causes soil erosion and pollution. Another danger is breaking off chunks of coral reefs by accident or on purpose. Boaters damaged this elkhorn coral.
pages.brief: Bleached corals stand pale as acidic ocean water dissolves their skeletons; destructive fishing with poisons and explosives, coastal building that causes soil erosion and pollution, and boaters breaking off chunks of elkhorn coral show other human harms to reefs.

pages.text: Protecting Coral Reefs Many countries have taken steps to protect nearby reefs. In some places, it is against the law to take fish, plants, or coral. People and boats are not allowed near many fragile reefs. But these laws are only a start. Coral Nurseries Scientists grow pieces of healthy coral in nurseries. The pieces may be rescued from boat damage or coastal building projects. Scientists hang the pieces from bars or place them in baskets. Later, they move the pieces to damaged reefs. The pieces help the reefs become healthy again.
pages.brief: In protected reef waters where laws keep people and boats away, scientists grow healthy coral pieces in an underwater nursery, hanging them from bars or placing them in baskets; later they move the rescued pieces to damaged reefs.

pages.text: Half of the world’s coral reefs have been destroyed. Most of those that remain are in trouble. Scientists are working to help coral reefs. We can help, too. Even if we don’t live near an ocean, we can do our part to reduce global warming. Using less energy, recycling, and walking or biking more all help. With our help, coral reefs will still be a beautiful natural wonder many years from now. What can you do to help?
pages.brief: A child walks with a bike beside a recycling bin and a house using less energy, while in the sea scientists tend coral and a healthy reef with fish remains a beautiful natural wonder for years to come.

books.title: Fantastic Flying Machines
books.art_why: Flying machines are real-world objects, and the book is not a biography of one famous person.

pages.text: People have always wanted to fly They watched birds fly They dreamed about how wonderful it would be A few people had good ideas about what made objects move through the air One man made a small toy propeller that could spin through the air In the 1400s, Leonardo da Vinci, an artist, drew amazing plans for a helicopter It might have worked— but he never built it People experimented Some strapped wings onto their arms and flapped A few tied themselves to big kites Almost everyone crashed over and over—but they wanted to fly! History of Flight In 1783, two French brothers invented the hot-air balloon Their first passengers were a sheep, a rooster, and a duck George Cayley built the first glider that carried a person Later, an engineer invented a better glider and published his ideas in 1889 A few years later, his ideas and notes inspired many of the designs of the Wright brothers.
pages.brief: A sequence of early-flight scenes: people watch birds and dream of flying; Leonardo da Vinci sketches a helicopter plan; experimenters strap on wings, flap, tie themselves to big kites, and crash. Two French brothers stand by a hot-air balloon carrying a sheep, a rooster, and a duck; George Cayley’s glider carries a person.

pages.text: Orville and Wilbur Wright thought about all these early ideas They thought about why most of them didn’t work After many tests, the Wright brothers built the first successful airplane that was powered by an engine It could carry only one person, so they took turns testing it On December 17, 1903, it was Orville’s turn That day, he flew for one full minute and went 260 meters (850 ft ) People could fly! Airplanes Planes have improved a lot since the early days of flight Large passenger airplanes are the first type of flying machine that most people see Have you flown in an airplane on a vacation trip? These types of planes can carry about 450 passengers and their luggage They can take you across the country or around the world.
pages.brief: Orville and Wilbur Wright work through tests and build a powered airplane. On December 17, 1903, Orville flies it for one full minute and covers 260 meters. Nearby, a large passenger airplane shows the later type most people see, able to carry about 450 passengers and their luggage across the country or around the world.

pages.text: Many planes that are built to fly high or fast use jet engines Jet engines are powerful They push an airplane forward by forcing a stream, or jet, of hot gas out behind them Some jets can fly faster than the speed of sound Many slower or older airplanes have propeller engines Each blade on a propeller acts like a wing The blades create air suction when they spin, like blades on a fan This force pulls the plane forward Stunt pilots use small propeller planes to do tricks at air shows Farmers use them to spray crops.
pages.brief: A jet engine pushes a fast plane forward with a stream of hot gas; another plane has a spinning propeller whose blades act like wings and pull it forward. A stunt pilot performs tricks in a small propeller plane at an air show, while a farmer uses a similar plane to spray crops.

pages.text: Some planes are built for a particular task Mail planes deliver packages overnight Military cargo planes move trucks, supplies, and troops Planes set up as offices allow people to work while they fly to business meetings Helicopters Helicopters are another common type of flying machine They can fly and land almost anywhere Most helicopters have two rotors The large rotor on top lifts the helicopter A smaller one on the tail helps the pilot steer Unlike planes, helicopters can fly backward and rotate They can even hover in midair!
pages.brief: A mail plane carries packages overnight; a military cargo plane holds trucks, supplies, and troops; an office plane lets people work during a business flight. Beside them, a helicopter with a large top rotor and a smaller tail rotor lifts off, steers, flies backward, rotates, and hovers in midair.

pages.text: Some helicopters are designed to lift heavy loads These helicopters need two rotors on top Firefighters sometimes use these helicopters to fight forest fires in remote areas Helicopters travel faster than cars Hospitals use helicopters as ambulances to reach injured people quickly Police use helicopters to patrol neighborhoods from the sky Rescue teams use them to look for people who are lost.
pages.brief: A heavy-lift helicopter with two rotors on top carries a large load. Firefighters use a helicopter to fight a forest fire in a remote area; a hospital helicopter acts as an ambulance reaching an injured person; police patrol neighborhoods from the sky; a rescue team searches for lost people.

pages.text: Blimps and Balloons Hot-air balloons fly very slowly They can’t be steered, so they drift where the wind pushes them Gas burners warm the air inside the balloons, making them rise in the colder air around them People fly in hot-air balloons for fun It’s a quiet and unusual way to see the countryside from above Blimps are flying machines that are often seen above large sporting events Blimps are large, long balloons filled with lighter-than-air gas, such as helium They usually have two small propeller engines and can be steered by a pilot—but they fly slowly Blimps attract attention, so companies put their names on them for advertising.
pages.brief: Hot-air balloons drift slowly where the wind pushes them, with gas burners warming the air inside so they rise in colder air; people ride one for fun and look down at the countryside. Nearby, a long blimp filled with helium floats above a large sporting event, with two small propeller engines and a pilot steering slowly.

pages.text: Rockets and Spaceships Rockets are very powerful engines that force hot gases out behind them to create thrust In 1957, the Soviet Union surprised the world when it used a rocket to launch the first satellite The satellite’s name was Sputnik It captured everyone’s imagination People thought about space travel—and being astronauts Since then, rockets have carried people to the Moon and have helped build a space station A space shuttle rides a rocket into space It carries astronauts and supplies to the International Space Station On its return trip to Earth, its wings let it land like an airplane.
pages.brief: A powerful rocket forces hot gases out behind it to create thrust. In 1957, the Soviet Union launches Sputnik, the first satellite; people imagine space travel and astronauts. Later, a rocket carries people to the Moon and helps build a space station, while a space shuttle rides a rocket upward with astronauts and supplies, then lands like an airplane.

pages.text: Other Ways to Fly Today, there are many ways to fly Hang gliders take off from cliffs and glide to the earth, drifting on air currents In sleek, thin glider aircraft, people can soar for hours Long ago, people could only imagine flying like birds Now, many people have the chance to fly Where would you like to fly? Index.
pages.brief: A hang glider takes off from a cliff and drifts on air currents toward the earth. Nearby, a sleek, thin glider aircraft soars for hours. Below, people enjoy different ways to fly, imagining where they would like to go, now that flying like birds is no longer only a dream.

books.title: Explorer's Guide to World Weather
books.art_why: The book is about real-world weather, Earth, climates, and measurable natural processes that exist today.

pages.text: Explorer’s Guide to World Weather Explorer’s Guide Explorer’s Guide to World Weather to World Weather Written by Celeste Fraser Written by Celeste Fraser Written by Celeste Fraser.
pages.brief: A cover page for an explorer’s guide to world weather, suggesting a journey across Earth’s climates. The design is clean and documentary-like, with a global exploration feel. No people or specific weather scene are shown; the page introduces the guide itself.

pages.text: Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: A simple opening spread for the world weather guide, with a clean documentary look. It establishes the guide’s subject without showing a specific place, person, or weather event. The page feels like a calm introduction before the details begin.

pages.text: Introducing Earth Oceans and air swirl around Earth. Ocean waters that wash the shores of North America also wash the shores of Asia. The breeze that blows curtains in South America rustles leaves in Africa’s trees. Yet regions on Earth can be very different from one another. In some places, people never need a heavy coat. In other places, people never go without one. Farmers pray for rain in some places. In other places, rain falls every day. Let’s look at why different parts of our planet have such different weather.
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth from space, showing oceans and air around the planet. Scenes suggest shared waters and breezes linking continents: curtains moving in a South American window and leaves rustling in African trees. People in some regions wear heavy coats; others never need one. Farmers look to the sky for rain.

pages.text: How Scientists Measure Weather How many words can you think of to describe weather? Hot, cold, warm, chilly, rainy, sunny, snowy, foggy —the list could go on and on. All these words describe two things: temperature and precipitation. Temperature is how hot or cold a place is. Precipitation is moisture that falls to the ground in the form of rain, snow, sleet, or hail. To track the weather of a place, we measure two things. How hot is it? How wet is it? Climate is the average weather in a place over long periods of time. Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: A scientist measures how hot and wet a place is. Words like hot, cold, warm, chilly, rainy, sunny, snowy, and foggy suggest temperature and precipitation. Moisture falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. The scientist compares how hot and how wet a place is over long periods to understand climate.

pages.text: Weather information can be recorded on graphs. Look at the temperature graph below. The graph shows information on the weather in Sydney, Australia, for the first six months of the year. The numbers on the left side show the degrees of temperature. Now look at the precipitation graph. It is very similar except that, on the left side, the numbers show amounts of precipitation in inches. Scientists have discovered that Earth has many different climate patterns by collecting weather information over time at many places.
pages.brief: A temperature graph for Sydney, Australia, shows six months of the year, with degrees marked on the left side. Beside it, a precipitation graph uses the same style, with inches marked on the left. Scientists compare weather information collected over time at many places to discover Earth’s different climate patterns.

pages.text: Why It’s Warmer Near the Equator Equator Climate Field Guide What affects Earth’s climate patterns? It all starts with the Sun. The Sun warms our planet, but its warmth is spread unevenly over Earth’s surface. The equator is an imaginary line that circles the middle of Earth like a belt. Areas near the equator tend to be much warmer than areas far to the north or south. Because Earth is shaped like a ball, the Sun’s rays hit Earth at different angles in different places. The Sun’s rays are most direct around Earth’s middle. They are least direct at the North and South Poles. Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: A view of Earth as a ball with an imaginary belt-like equator around its middle. The Sun’s rays strike Earth at different angles: most direct near the equator and least direct at the North and South Poles. This shows why areas near the equator tend to be warmer than far northern or southern regions.

pages.text: Try This! Mark an X in the center of a sheet of paper. Have a friend hold the paper so it’s facing you. Shine a flashlight at the paper so it makes a circle of light around the X. Have your friend slowly tilt the paper away from you. As the paper is tilted away, the circle of light will stretch to become an oval. The same amount of light is being spread over more of the paper. Even though the X is still in the light, it is now getting less light than it was before. In the same way, as you move north or south away from the equator, Earth curves more and more away from the Sun. Earth’s polar regions are cold because they receive less direct sunlight than areas near the equator.
pages.brief: A hands-on experiment with a sheet of paper, a friend, and a flashlight. The flashlight makes a circle of light around a mark in the paper’s center. The friend slowly tilts the paper away, stretching the circle into an oval. The same light spreads over more paper, so the mark receives less light.

pages.text: The latitude and longitude system of grid lines makes it possible to describe the location of any spot on Earth. Degrees of latitude measure distance north or south of the equator. Degrees of longitude measure distance east or west of Greenwich, England. Latitude Latitude is the system we use for measuring distance north and south of the equator. The equator is 0 degrees (0°) latitude. The North Pole is 90 degrees north latitude; the South Pole is 90 degrees south latitude. The smaller the latitude measurement, the closer a place is to the equator. The greater the latitude measurement, the farther it is from the equator. Climates at or near the equator are generally warm. Climates far from the equator are generally cold. Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: A globe marked with a grid of latitude and longitude lines. Degrees of latitude measure distance north or south of the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at the poles. Smaller latitude numbers lie closer to the warm equator; greater numbers lie farther away, where climates are generally colder.

pages.text: Elevation Elevation is the height above or below sea level. It can affect climate. Imagine you were at the equator standing on a high mountaintop. You would be in a cold climate! That’s because the temperature of the air drops about three degrees Fahrenheit for every 1,000 feet the elevation increases. Mountains can also affect precipitation. Air contains water vapor —water in the form of a gas. Air tends to move around the planet in certain directions, called prevailing winds. When wind hits a chain of mountains, the air is forced upward, where it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much moisture as warm air. So air drops its moisture (as rain, snow, sleet, or hail) on the windward side of the mountains. That leaves the other side, the leeward side, very dry. Dry regions caused by mountain “walls” are called rain shadows. Warm, moist air Forest Sea Region of rain shadow Dry air Desert.
pages.brief: A high mountaintop at the equator, where air is cold despite the tropical location. Mountains force moist wind upward; the cooling air drops rain, snow, sleet, or hail on the windward side. The leeward side stays dry as a rain shadow. Warm, moist air rises from forest near the sea; dry air reaches desert beyond the mountains.

pages.text: Large Bodies of Water Large bodies of water affect temperature and precipitation. Water heats up and cools down more slowly than the land. So, large bodies of water act as a kind of insulation on the areas of land next to them. They keep the land from heating up or cooling down too quickly. Places near large bodies of water have mild winters and summers. By contrast, places that are far from large bodies of water often have very cold winters and very hot summers. In those places, the air does not hold enough water vapor to act as insulation. Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: Land beside a large body of water, where the water heats and cools more slowly than the land. This keeps nearby places from heating up or cooling down too quickly, giving them mild winters and summers. Farther inland, away from the water, winters can be very cold and summers very hot because the air holds less water vapor.

pages.text: Ocean currents also play a part in climate. Cold water currents flow from the poles toward the equator. Warm water currents do the opposite, flowing from the equator toward the poles. Air above these currents slowly becomes the same temperature as the water. So, if a prevailing wind blows from water to land, it generally warms or cools those regions. With its high latitude, Western Europe should have a fairly cold climate. However, a warm water current called the North Atlantic Drift warms the air above it. This gives Western Europe a milder climate. This current also gives the region a wet climate. Because warm air can carry more moisture than cool air, the air that floats over Europe is loaded with water vapor. People in this rainy part of the world need raincoats and umbrellas. A Warm Water Current A Warm Water Current.
pages.brief: Ocean currents move cold water from the poles toward the equator and warm water from the equator toward the poles. Air above the water takes on its temperature. A warm current, the North Atlantic Drift, warms the air above it and gives Western Europe a milder, wetter climate; people there need raincoats and umbrellas.

pages.text: How Earth’s Tilt Causes Its Seasons Axis Spring Axis tilts away from Sun Axis tilts toward Sun Fall Equator Northern Winter Northern Summer Winter Summer Sun Sunlight more direct above equator Sunlight more direct below equator Summer Winter Fall Earth orbits the Sun once each year. Spring Seasons Most climates along the equator are hot all year round because of the direct sunlight they receive. Climates in other places on Earth change with the seasons because of Earth’s tilt. Look at the diagram above. In January, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. That causes winter there. In July, it is tilted toward the Sun, which causes summer. The Southern Hemisphere has opposite seasons because it tilts in the opposite direction from the Northern Hemisphere. Explorer’s Guide to World Weather.
pages.brief: Earth orbiting the Sun with its axis tilted. In January the Northern Hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, causing winter there; in July it tilts toward the Sun, causing summer. The Southern Hemisphere has opposite seasons. Equatorial climates stay hot all year because sunlight is more direct above the equator.

pages.text: A green valley in the Alps mountain range in Central Europe Exploring Earth’s Climate Patterns You’ve just had a quick tour of the forces that affect Earth’s climates. Pick a place on a globe. Think about the things that affect its climate. How far is it from the equator? Is its elevation high or low? Are there mountains or large bodies of water nearby? What season is it there right now? If you can answer these questions, you can probably guess what the weather is like there, even without leaving your home!
pages.brief: A green valley in the Alps mountain range in Central Europe. The valley lies among high mountains, showing a real place where elevation, mountains, and location shape climate. The scene invites the reader to choose a place on a globe and think about distance from the equator, elevation, nearby mountains or water, and the current season.

pages.text: (n.) page 10 winds that generally blow in a specific direction rain shadows (n.) page 10 areas that have a dry climate because they are on the leeward side of a mountain range regions (n.) page 4 places, locations, or areas temperature (n.) page 5 the measurement of how hot or cold a place is water vapor (n.) page 10 water in the form of a gas windward (adj.) page 10 the side on the direction from which the wind is coming Index.
pages.brief: A clean end-of-book reference page for weather terms, arranged as a glossary and index. It organizes key words from the guide into short entries, giving the book a tidy close. No scenic illustration or person appears, keeping the focus on the guide’s useful reference material.

books.title: Critter Crossings
books.art_why: Modern animals, highways, and real ecopassages can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Imagine you are a turtle stuck on one side of a six-lane freeway. On the other side is food, room to roam, and maybe even a mate. Huge metal monsters race past you. They move much faster than you ever can. How can you hope to safely cross without being flattened?
pages.brief: A turtle sits at the edge of a wide six-lane freeway, looking across at food, open ground, and another turtle on the far side. Huge cars and trucks race past in a blur, much faster than the turtle can walk.

pages.text: Many animals—not just turtles—face the dangers of crossing roads every day. Some make it across, while others don’t. Humans can help these animals safely move to the other side by building critter crossings, or ecopassages. They come in many different types, but they all help animals—including humans—stay alive.
pages.brief: Many different animals gather near a roadway, some crossing while others wait at the edge. Nearby, people have built animal crossings of different types, giving animals and humans a safer way to stay alive.

pages.text: Banff Is the Best Banff National Park in Canada has some of the most beautiful mountains in North America. It also has the Trans-Canada Highway running through it. During the busy summer, the highway may carry more than 25,000 vehicles each day. It used to be the site of hundreds of collisions between animals and vehicles each year.
pages.brief: The Trans-Canada Highway runs through Banff National Park in Canada, with beautiful mountains rising behind it. More than 25,000 vehicles travel the busy summer road each day, and animals are shown near the roadside where collisions happen.

pages.text: Then Parks Canada built over thirty animal underpasses and overpasses (with more planned for the future). The crossings cost millions of dollars and raised an important question: what if the animals didn’t use them? Keeping Track People use different methods to keep track of animals using the crossings. Cameras at some crossings take pictures whenever an animal uses them. Other crossings use soft dirt or sand track pads. Animals leave footprints on these pads when they pass through. Humans can study the tracks in the pads before raking them clean.
pages.brief: Over thirty animal underpasses and overpasses cross the highway in Banff, built by Parks Canada. A camera watches one crossing while a person studies footprints in a soft dirt track pad before raking it clean.

pages.text: Species Overpass Underpass That first year, only one black bear and one mountain lion used the Banff crossings—one time each. Today, however, all sorts of animals move above and below the highway. As of 2011, animals have used the passes to cross more than 220,000 times.
pages.brief: A black bear walks over a Banff wildlife overpass while a mountain lion moves through an underpass below. Other animals use the crossings too, moving above and below the highway that carries traffic through the park.

pages.text: Look Out for the Little Guy Massachusetts created the first U.S. tunnels for the spotted salamander. Each year, these endangered animals migrate from the forest, across a busy street, to the water to mate. Two narrow tunnels under the road now let them migrate in safety.
pages.brief: Spotted salamanders leave a forest in Massachusetts and head toward water to mate, facing a busy street. Two narrow tunnels beneath the road let the endangered amphibians migrate safely, moving under the traffic instead of across it.

pages.text: Florida wanted to save the lives of thousands of snakes, frogs, and other small animals. So the state built walls along either side of U.S. 441. Each wall is 42 inches (107 cm) high. At the top of each wall is a 6-inch (15 cm) lip that these small animals cannot climb over. This lip keeps the animals off the surface of the road. Tunnels underneath the road help the animals cross to the other side.
pages.brief: Along a Florida highway, walls 42 inches high, each with a 6-inch lip at the top, keep snakes, frogs, and other small animals from climbing onto the road. The small animals move along the wall and enter tunnels underneath the road to cross safely.

pages.text: Why Bother? Building these crossings costs millions of dollars, which some might argue is too much money. Consider this: each year in the United States, there are more than one million collisions between vehicles and animals. These crashes kill over 200 people per year and cost billions of dollars in repairs, cleanup, and hospital bills. Building more animal crossings would lower the number of crashes. For example, the crossings in Banff cut the number of animals killed by vehicles by more than 80 percent. The smaller number of collisions saves money and the lives of humans and many other animals.
pages.brief: A damaged car sits at the roadside after a collision with an animal on a highway. In the distance, a Banff wildlife overpass crosses the road, showing a safer crossing that can lower crashes, save money, and protect people and animals.

pages.text: Even More Reasons Sometimes these crossings can save animals from extinction. The number of grizzly bears in Banff is very low. A few adult females killed on the road could have meant the end of these bears in the park. Thanks to the passages, though, the grizzly bears can cross the highway safely. For other endangered animals, a safe crossing may not only save the animal, but the entire species.
pages.brief: A female grizzly bear walks across a Banff wildlife overpass above the highway, with mountains behind her. The crossing lets this bear move safely through the park, helping a very small grizzly population avoid disappearing from the area.

pages.text: Ecopassages also help large animals find food. Mountain lions and bears may roam hundreds of miles during the year to find prey. Roads can cut up habitats and sometimes keep animals from being able to move freely. Species that can’t cross roads to reach food have less of a chance to survive.
pages.brief: A mountain lion and a bear roam near a highway that cuts through their habitat, searching for prey over a wide area. An ecopassage lets large animals move between divided stretches of land so they can reach food and survive.

pages.text: Animals need to find mates, as well. Roads can keep members of the same species apart. If they can’t find a mate, they can’t have babies. Without babies, a species can quickly disappear from an area. In some cases, it can even lead to the extinction of a species.
pages.brief: Two animals of the same species stand on opposite sides of a busy road, separated by the traffic. Without a safe way to reach each other, they cannot mate or have babies, and their kind can disappear from the area.

pages.text: Conclusion Imagine you are the turtle again. The metal monsters race by. This time, though, someone has built an animal crossing. You happen to look down and spot a tunnel that leads underneath the road. You slowly make your way toward the tunnel. You are safe for one more day. Did You Know? Some turtles can take more than seven hours to cross a two-lane road!
pages.brief: The turtle waits at the edge of a busy road as cars and trucks race past. It looks down and sees a tunnel leading underneath the road, then slowly moves toward it, safe for one more day.

books.title: Woods of Wonder
books.art_why: Old-growth forests and their animals exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Woods of Wonder.
pages.brief: A deep old-growth forest fills the view, with tall trunks, a layered green canopy, ferns, moss, and fallen logs; soft sunlight filters through the leaves, and no people are visible in the peaceful, distant woods.

pages.text: Oh, That’s Old! Old-growth forests look very different from one another. Some have only one kind of tree. Others have many kinds of trees. Some may have very tall trees. Others have trees that are short.
pages.brief: A wide view of old-growth forest shows variety: one area has trees of a single kind, another has many kinds mixed together, with some very tall trees and other shorter trees of different shapes beneath.

pages.text: These forests are so different that scientists do not have one definition for old-growth forests. Yet many old-growth forests do have things in common. Many scientists think that an old-growth forest must be at least 150 years old. Not every tree in the forest has to be that old, though.
pages.brief: Two scientists stand among old-growth trees, looking closely at a massive trunk; around them, some trees are very old and others are younger and thinner, showing a forest where not every tree is 150 years old.

pages.text: Forest Levels The canopy should have more than one layer. The tallest trees form the top layer. Fallen trees make holes in the canopy where sunlight gets through. Young trees can grow in these holes. Dead trees give food and shelter to many living things. Old-growth forests are home to plants and animals that can’t live anywhere else. If we study and care for these forests, we can learn a lot.
pages.brief: A layered old-growth forest shows the canopy: tallest trees form a top layer; a gap left by a fallen tree lets sunlight reach young trees below; a dead log on the forest floor shelters small living things.

pages.text: United States California has many great national parks, some with old-growth forests. In Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks, coniferous trees make up most of the old-growth forests. Giant sequoias grow here, and one of these giants is the largest tree in the world. A sequoia can live for more than 3,000 years.
pages.brief: A giant sequoia towers in a coniferous old-growth forest in California; its massive reddish trunk rises past smaller trees, and its very high crown reaches above the others in Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks.

pages.text: The Pacific fisher also lives in the park. Its favorite meal is porcupine. Because it only lives in old-growth forests, some states are trying to protect it. Tough, Not Tall Not all old-growth forests have towering trees. In some harsh places with wild and icy winds, pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees grow short and twisted. These trees are called Krummholz, a German word meaning “crooked wood.” They are only about 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, but don’t let their size fool you. Some are one thousand years old.
pages.brief: A Pacific fisher, a dark furry mammal, stands on a branch in an old-growth forest near a porcupine; beyond, on a harsh windy slope, short twisted Krummholz pines and spruces bend sideways, only about six feet tall.

pages.text: Across the country in North Carolina and Tennessee is Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Old-growth forests make up only a small part of this park. These forests are mostly made up of deciduous trees.
pages.brief: A misty mountain landscape in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, across North Carolina and Tennessee; a small patch of old-growth deciduous forest with broad-leaf trees stands among younger woods, showing that old growth is only a small part of the park.

pages.text: Endangered Carolina northern flying squirrels live here. These animals do not actually fly. They use skin attached to their front and back paws to glide. These animals are in danger because people have cut down other forests where they could live.
pages.brief: An endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel spreads its paws and glides between trees in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the skin flaps between its front and back paws stretched wide; below, a forest and a few cut stumps show lost habitat.

pages.text: Japan Shirakami-Sanchi is one of the last old- growth forests in East Asia. It is a small area in the northern mountains of Japan. Forests like this one once covered most of northern Japan.
pages.brief: A small old-growth forest fills a mountain valley in northern Japan, in Shirakami-Sanchi; dense green trees and mist cover the slopes, while surrounding ridges stretch beyond, hinting at forests that once covered most of northern Japan.

pages.text: The forest is home to a rare kind of serow. This goatlike animal is only found here and in two other small areas in Japan. Black woodpeckers also live here. These birds are endangered in Japan.
pages.brief: A goatlike serow stands quietly on a rocky forest slope in Shirakami-Sanchi; nearby, a black woodpecker clings to a trunk, its dark feathers against the bark, in this small rare old-growth forest of northern Japan.

pages.text: Russia The Western Caucasus in Russia has many forests that are mostly made up of coniferous trees. It is home to many different plants and animals.
pages.brief: A dense green coniferous forest deep in the Western Caucasus Mountains of Russia, with tall pines and firs, mossy shady ground, and many different plants and animals living quietly among the wide trunks and branches.

pages.text: Some scientists think that a few endangered snow leopards live here. Scientists sometimes find paw prints and other signs. The endangered wisent has also been brought back into the forest.
pages.brief: A scientist kneels in a snowy mountain forest, examining a large paw print in the snow; farther among the conifers, an endangered wisent stands quietly beside mossy trunks and rocks, while paw prints trail into the trees.

pages.text: Conclusion Old-growth forests may be hundreds or thousands of years old. Many of these places are protected, but some are in danger. Humans can damage or destroy them. Once gone, these old-growth forests may never return.
pages.brief: An ancient, quiet old-growth forest with massive, centuries-old trees; at its nearby edge, a cleared area with cut stumps and bare soil shows how humans can damage such forests, which may never return once destroyed.

books.title: Roadside Oddities
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing for this collection of roadside oddities.

pages.text: What Is The Thing? Driving between Texas and Arizona, you can’t miss the signs for The Thing. Giant billboards at the side of the road ask, “The Thing? What is it?” Whatever else it is, The Thing is one of thousands of roadside attractions around the world. Roadside attractions are weird and wonderful. They invite people to stop and check them out.
pages.brief: A long highway runs between Texas and Arizona under a wide sky. A car travels past several giant billboards standing at the roadside, and the driver and passengers look toward the signs as they approach.

pages.text: World’s Largest Baseball Bat The world’s largest baseball bat leans over a five- story building in Kentucky. The bat is 120 feet (37 m) tall and weighs more than 68,000 pounds (30,844 kg). It’s a huge replica of the bat used by the famous baseball player Babe Ruth.
pages.brief: In Kentucky, an enormous baseball bat leans over a five-story building. The towering bat is a huge replica of the bat used by famous baseball player Babe Ruth, and it rises high above the street beside the building.

pages.text: The Corn Palace At the Corn Palace in South Dakota, they create art out of corn. Every year, the outside of the building is decorated with local grains and grasses. The Corn Palace is also the world’s largest bird feeder. When winter begins, the birds and squirrels eat the art!
pages.brief: The Corn Palace in South Dakota rises with outside walls decorated in patterns made from local grains and grasses. In early winter, birds and squirrels gather on the building and eat pieces of the corn artwork, while the decorated palace stands under a cold sky.

pages.text: Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum Do you have a spare toilet seat lying around the house? If so, you can bring it to Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum in Texas. Barney opened the museum in 1992. It holds more than one thousand toilet seats Barney Smith has made into works of art.
pages.brief: Inside Barney Smith’s Toilet Seat Art Museum in Texas, more than one thousand toilet seats are displayed as works of art. The decorated seats fill the museum, showing Barney Smith’s creations in a crowded, colorful collection for visitors to see.

pages.text: Lucy the Elephant In 1881, James Lafferty built the world’s largest elephant in New Jersey. Lucy is a six-story building covered with 12,000 square feet (3,658 sq m) of metal. You can still climb inside Lucy the Elephant today.
pages.brief: Lucy the Elephant, a six-story building shaped like a giant elephant, stands in New Jersey covered with metal. Visitors climb up inside the huge elephant structure, which rises beside the road as a famous roadside attraction.

pages.text: Boll Weevil Monument In 1915, a bug called the boll weevil destroyed cotton crops in Alabama. It forced farmers to grow different types of plants, such as peanuts. In the end, growing other crops helped farmers. So they built a monument to honor the weevil.
pages.brief: In Alabama, a monument honors the boll weevil, the bug that destroyed cotton crops in 1915. Around the monument, a cotton field and peanut plants show how farmers switched crops after the weevil forced them to grow different plants.

pages.text: Sign Post Forest If you’re driving along the Alaska Highway, you’ll find a forest that isn’t made of trees. Sign Post Forest in northwest Canada is made of more than 100,000 signs. People have been hanging signs there since 1942. Do You Know? Not all roadside attractions are made by people. General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park is the world’s largest tree by volume. It is estimated to be between 2,300 and 2,700 years old.
pages.brief: Along the Alaska Highway in northwest Canada, a roadside forest of more than one hundred thousand signs stands where people have hung signs since 1942. A separate view shows the massive General Sherman Tree, the world’s largest tree by volume, towering in Sequoia National Park.

pages.text: Carhenge In Nebraska, you can visit a replica of England’s Stonehenge. It was built in 1987, not with old stones, but with thirty-eight old cars. Some people once wanted the spot turned into a junkyard. Now more than 80,000 people visit it each year.
pages.brief: In Nebraska, thirty-eight old cars stand upright in a circle to form Carhenge, a replica of England’s Stonehenge. The rusty car bodies create arches and pillars in an open field, and visitors walk among the unusual monument.

pages.text: London Bridge Where is London Bridge? In Arizona, of course. While a number of roadside attractions are replicas, this one is the real deal. The London Bridge was first built in 1831. In 1968, an American bought it for $2,460,000. He had to spend another $7 million to have the bridge taken apart and moved to Arizona.
pages.brief: The real London Bridge, first built in 1831, stands in Arizona after being taken apart and moved from England. Its stone arches and towers rise in the Arizona landscape, where visitors can walk across the historic bridge.

pages.text: World’s Largest Basket Workers at a basket company in Ohio get to work inside a basket that’s seven stories tall. The building is a replica of one of their baskets. When it was first built, a pilot flew his small plane through the handles!
pages.brief: A seven-story building shaped like a giant basket stands in Ohio, a replica of one of the company’s baskets. Workers get to work inside the huge basket, and a small plane is shown flying through the handles when it was first built.

pages.text: World’s Largest (You Name It) 1 World’s largest tire, Allen Park, Michigan 2 World’s largest chest of drawers, High Point, North Carolina 3 World’s largest violin, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, Canada • World’s largest artichoke, Castroville, California • World’s largest ketchup bottle, Collinsville, Illinois • World’s largest cuckoo clock, Sugarcreek, Ohio • World’s largest ear of corn, Olivia, Minnesota • World’s largest rubber stamp, Cleveland, Ohio.
pages.brief: A playful lineup of giant roadside objects appears beside different roads: a tire in Michigan, a chest of drawers in North Carolina, a violin in Nova Scotia, an artichoke in California, a ketchup bottle in Illinois, a cuckoo clock in Ohio, an ear of corn in Minnesota, and a rubber stamp in Cleveland.

pages.text: A Map to Amazement UNITED STATES ATLANTIC OCEAN MEXICO Stop and Look Roadside attractions have one thing in common. They grab people’s attention and cause them to stop. Do you want to know what The Thing is, off the highway in Arizona? You’ll just have to pull off the road to find out!
pages.brief: A simplified map shows the United States beside the Atlantic Ocean and Mexico. A highway leads to a roadside attraction in Arizona, where a car pulls off the road, and travelers stop to look at the mysterious Thing.

books.title: Animal Discoveries
books.art_why: Real animals exist today and can be photographed; no named famous person is involved.

pages.text: Animal Discoveries.
pages.brief: A calm opening spread with no specific people or animals named on this page. Soft natural light and a simple background suggest the start of a book about animal discoveries, leaving the space open for the subject to come next.

pages.text: Animals have scientific names. This jellyfish is called Tamoya ohboya. The name was chosen in a contest. The winner said most people would say “Oh boy!” when seeing the jellyfish. Introduction If you wanted to find a new animal species, where would you look? You might look in remote corners of the globe. Scientists find more than 15,000 animal species each year. That’s 1 percent of the more than 1.5 million species we know about already. At the same time, species are dying out at record rates around the globe. For this reason, when we do stumble on a new species, it is an important discovery.
pages.brief: A Tamoya ohboya jellyfish floats in dark ocean water, its bell and tentacles visible. The jellyfish is the only subject, shown clearly so its shape and details can be seen. The setting is underwater, with no other animals or people around it.

pages.text: Monkey Mania In 2007, a new species of monkey was found in the forests of Central Africa. The lesula has large eyes and is shy and quiet. The first one found by scientists was being kept as a pet. In 2010, scientists found the Caquetá titi monkey by listening to its calls. This monkey lives in the Amazon jungle. The Caquetá is known for its bushy red beard. It doesn’t have a white bar on its forehead as other titi monkeys do. Its babies purr like cats. Only around 250 Caquetá titi monkeys are alive today, meaning the species is endangered.
pages.brief: In a Central African forest, a lesula monkey with large eyes sits quietly, shy and calm. Nearby, in the Amazon jungle, a Caquetá titi monkey with a bushy red beard and no white forehead bar clings to a branch; a tiny baby titi rests close by.

pages.text: Freaky, Fabulous Frogs The Matang narrow-mouthed frog is the size of a pea. It was discovered on the island of Borneo in 2010. It turns out that scientists had seen these frogs before. They thought the frogs were the young of a different species. Then, they heard the frogs calling. Since only adult frogs make calls, they realized that these tiny frogs must be full-grown.
pages.brief: A tiny Matang narrow-mouthed frog, about the size of a pea, sits on a leaf on Borneo. Nearby, scientists listen as the small frog calls, realizing it is a full-grown adult rather than the young of another species.

pages.text: A scientist discovered the long-nosed tree frog in 2010. This frog lives in the Foja Mountains of New Guinea. The area has been called the “Lost World.” This tree frog is known for its long nose. It is sometimes called the Pinocchio frog. When the male frog calls, its nose points up. When the frog is done calling, its nose falls. No one knows why.
