pages.brief: A male long-nosed tree frog sits on a branch in the misty Foja Mountains of New Guinea. Its long nose points upward as it calls. The forest around it is lush and remote, with no people or other animals.

pages.text: Furry Finds Another find during the 2010 Foja Mountains trip was the blossom bat. It uses its long tongue to drink nectar from flowers. During a 2005 trip to Madagascar, researchers found Goodman’s mouse lemurs. Not much bigger than mice, these tiny lemurs jump around in the trees at night. During the daytime, they sometimes sleep in empty birds’ nests. Do You Know? Lemurs are only found in Madagascar.
pages.brief: A blossom bat hovers by a flower, its long tongue reaching for nectar. In a Madagascar forest, tiny Goodman’s mouse lemurs leap through trees at night; one curls up to sleep in an empty bird’s nest during the day.

pages.text: Interesting Invertebrates Scientists think that vertebrates—animals with backbones—make up only 3 percent of all species. The remaining 97 percent of animal species known to scientists are invertebrates— animals without backbones. Sazima’s tarantula has a special beauty. Its dark blue body almost glows. This fantastic arachnid has a limited habitat. It only lives high in the mountains of Brazil.
pages.brief: A Sazima’s tarantula rests high in the mountains of Brazil. Its dark blue body looks almost glowing in the mountain setting. The tarantula is shown alone in its limited habitat, with no people or other animals nearby.

pages.text: Discovered in 2013 in South America, this new type of planthopper looks strange. The wild hair isn’t hair at all. When an enemy attacks, the “hair” breaks off, and the planthopper can jump to safety. That’s what scientists think, anyway, but they aren’t sure.
pages.brief: A newly discovered planthopper clings to a plant in South America. Strange wild strands look like hair on its body. The insect is shown close up, with its odd covering visible, in a green setting with no people or other animals.

pages.text: Underwater Wonders Scientists found the Gorgon’s head starfish in 2010 in the Atlantic Ocean. The Gorgon’s head, a type of basket star, has five arms that split off from its body. The five arms have as many as five thousand tips. The tips help it find food floating by in the water. It also uses its arms to walk along the ocean bottom and to protect itself.
pages.brief: A Gorgon’s head starfish, a basket star, rests on the Atlantic Ocean bottom. Five arms branch out from its body, ending in many fine tips. The starfish uses its arms to move along the seafloor and reach for food floating in the water.

pages.text: It took until 2013 to find the walking bamboo shark. Like most sharks, it is no threat to humans. It lives off the coast of Indonesia. Scientists found it because the colors on its back are different from those of other sharks. This new species uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor in search of food. The wiggling movement makes it look as though the shark is walking.
pages.brief: A walking bamboo shark moves along the ocean floor off the coast of Indonesia. It uses its fins to push itself forward in a wiggling motion that looks like walking. Its back shows unusual colors, and it searches for food in the water.

pages.text: Hiding in Plain View For more than a hundred years, scientists thought the olinguito (oh-lin-GEE-toh) was another species. In 2013, they discovered that they had been wrong. The olinguito leaps through trees at night. The smallest member of the raccoon family, it can be found in South America. Mistaken Identity Humans may encounter an unidentified species for years while mistaking it for a familiar species. This often happens because the two species look the same, at least on the outside. These are called cryptic species. They are only found to be distinct when scientists study their genetic code. As DNA technology is used more and more, reports of distinct new species are on the rise.
pages.brief: An olinguito leaps through trees at night in South America. The small, raccoon-family animal is shown in motion among branches. In the dark forest, it is the only creature visible, with no people or other animals around.

pages.text: In 2009, researchers found the Cambodian tailorbird. Tests showed that this tailorbird was a new species. Scientists also studied the bird’s song. While all tailorbirds sing, no two species sound the same. Sure enough, the song of the Cambodian tailorbird is different from all the rest.
pages.brief: A Cambodian tailorbird perches on a branch and sings. The small bird is shown with its beak open in song. The setting is simple and natural, with no other animals or people visible nearby. It is the only subject on the page.

pages.text: Number of Species Discovered by Type 2000–2009 1 Insects 88,598 2 Plants 23,604 3 Arachnids 12,751 4 Fungi 11,984 5 Crustaceans 7,070 6 Mollusks 5,949 7 Bacteria 4,417 8 Fish 3,587 9 All other 18,351 What’s Next? Scientists continue to amaze us by finding new species. Experts agree that many more have yet to be found. Many of these newly found species are in danger of dying out. Finding them means we can help save their homes. Doing this can save the animals that live there, both those we know about and those we don’t know about…yet.
pages.brief: A wide natural scene shows examples of discovered species: insects, plants, an arachnid, fungi, a crustacean, a mollusk, and a fish. Scientists continue searching for more, and many of these creatures live in habitats that need protection.

books.title: The Mighty Mississippi
books.art_why: The Mississippi River, its wildlife, locks, dams and modern structures are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi.
pages.brief: A wide, powerful river fills the view, with broad water stretching between low banks under a large sky. The current looks strong and steady, and the river seems to go on for a very long distance. No boats or people appear.

pages.text: Clouds gather above Minnesota’s Lake Itasca. An Epic Journey Rain falls on Lake Itasca in Minnesota. It mixes into the clear waters of a river so small that a child could wade across it. This is the start of the mighty Mississippi River. A Lake of Many Names Lake Itasca is just one name for the lake where the Mississippi River begins. The Ojibwe people, who first lived in the area, called the lake Omashkoozo-zaaga’igan.
pages.brief: Clouds gather above Lake Itasca in Minnesota, and rain falls onto the lake. The rainwater mixes into the clear, shallow water of a tiny river so small that a child could wade across it. This small stream is the beginning of the Mississippi River.

pages.text: The Mississippi Watershed Lake Itasca United States GULF OF MEXICO A watershed is the area that drains into a river or lake. The Mississippi River watershed is the fourth largest in the world. It includes many U.S. states and a bit of Canada. Many other rivers flow into the Mississippi. One of them— the Missouri—is even longer than the Mississippi! Over the next three months, the water will take a 2,350-mile (3,781 km) journey through ten U.S. states. It will flow past plants, animals, cities, towns, and farmland. It will carry food and other items to people up and down the river. At last, it will enter the Gulf of Mexico.
pages.brief: A wide landscape shows the Mississippi watershed as a huge area draining into the river, covering many U.S. states and a bit of Canada. Several rivers flow into the Mississippi, including the long Missouri. The river's path runs past plants, animals, cities, towns, and farmland toward the Gulf of Mexico.

pages.text: The Upper River After leaving the lake, the water flows through dozens of locks and dams. They work together to raise or lower the water around boats. This way boats can travel safely as water levels change. They also hold back water so boats don’t hit the river bottom.
pages.brief: On the upper river, boats move through a series of locks and dams built across the water. The structures raise or lower the water around each boat so it can travel safely as water levels change. They also hold back water to keep boats from hitting the river bottom.

pages.text: Barge Basics 1 Barge = 15 Train Cars = 58 Trucks Boats on this part of the river carry corn and soybeans south. Much of this food is shipped around the world.
pages.brief: A long river barge loaded with corn and soybeans moves south on the Mississippi. Beside it, fifteen train cars and fifty-eight trucks show the same amount of cargo, making clear how much one barge can carry. The food is later shipped around the world.

pages.text: More than fifty types of mammals live along the upper river. Playful river otters hunt and swim here. Oldies but Goodies At least 260 kinds of fish—25 percent of all fish types in North America—live in the Mississippi River. One kind is the pallid sturgeon, one of the oldest fish on Earth. It has hardly changed in 70 million years.
pages.brief: In the upper river, playful river otters hunt and swim in the water. Below the surface, many fish live, including the pallid sturgeon, an ancient fish that has hardly changed in seventy million years. The river is full of life along this stretch.

pages.text: A few miles north of St. Louis, Missouri, the muddy Missouri River comes in from the west. It mixes with the clear waters of the Mississippi and passes along its nickname: “The Big Muddy.” The Mississippi grows wide here, too.
pages.brief: A few miles north of St. Louis, Missouri, the muddy Missouri River comes in from the west. Its brown water mixes with the clear Mississippi River, and the combined river grows wide. The meeting of the two waters makes the river look muddy.

pages.text: For the next 190 miles (306 km), the river runs through areas with many wild animals. Bald eagles nest in the tall trees and eat the fish that swim in the river.
pages.brief: For the next 190 miles, the river runs through wild areas where many animals live. Bald eagles nest in tall trees beside the water. From their nests and branches, the eagles watch the river and eat fish that swim below.

pages.text: The Lower River Next, the Ohio River comes in from the east and joins the Mississippi. The amount of water doubles, and the river grows wider still. In many spots, it stretches 1.5 miles (2.4 km) from bank to bank. By the time the river reaches Louisiana, the Mississippi is very deep. It is deep enough in some places to cover the Statue of Liberty.
pages.brief: The Ohio River comes in from the east and joins the Mississippi, doubling the amount of water. The river grows wider, stretching about 1.5 miles from bank to bank in many places. By Louisiana, it is very deep, deep enough in some spots to cover the Statue of Liberty.

pages.text: Do You Know? The Statue of Liberty is 151 feet (46 m) tall without her base and pedestal. At its deepest, the Mississippi is about 200 feet (61 m) deep. The river’s depth changes from year to year. The Lower Mississippi has no dams. It does have a system to contain floods, but some floods are just too big. In fact, the Mississippi is famous for its floods, which sometimes destroy buildings and even kill people.
pages.brief: A cross-section shows the Statue of Liberty, 151 feet tall without her base, beside the deepest part of the Mississippi, about 200 feet deep. The river's depth changes from year to year. On the lower river, floodwater overwhelms a containment system and surrounds damaged buildings.

pages.text: Yet not all floods are bad. Along the river’s banks, the rich soil that the floods leave behind makes good farmland for cotton and grains. Along the lower part of the river, more cities rise up. From Tennessee and Louisiana, boats carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, and wood. They carry farm crops such as cotton from the area, too. Some items move north, back up the river, and some move farther south.
pages.brief: Floodwaters leave behind rich soil along the riverbanks, making good farmland for cotton and grains. More cities rise along the lower river. From Tennessee and Louisiana, boats carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, wood, and farm crops such as cotton, moving some goods north and some farther south.

pages.text: Several types of turtles call this part of the river home. So does the American alligator. Swimming All Summer Even humans swim in the river sometimes. In the summer of 2002, Slovenian long-distance swimmer Martin Strel swam the entire length of the river in sixty-eight days.
pages.brief: Several turtles and an American alligator share the lower river. A human swimmer, Slovenian long-distance swimmer Martin Strel, swims through the wide water. In the summer of 2002, he swam the entire length of the Mississippi River in sixty-eight days.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi.
pages.brief: A wide, powerful stretch of the Mississippi River fills the scene, with broad water moving between distant banks under an open sky. The river looks immense and steady, carrying its long journey toward the end. No boats or people are visible.

books.title: Dragonflies!
books.art_why: Real dragonflies, people, and habitats exist today, so photographs suit the book.

pages.text: Amazing Dragonflies Imagine that you’re walking past a lake or stream when suddenly— bzzt! —something big, shiny, and green zooms past your head. It’s bigger than a bumblebee, and it’s faster than a butterfly. It’s an amazing dragonfly!
pages.brief: A child walks beside a lake or stream when a big, shiny green dragonfly zooms past their head. The dragonfly is larger than a bumblebee and faster than a butterfly, making it an amazing sight.

pages.text: What Are Dragonflies? Dragonflies are flying insects with long bodies and two pairs of wings. They come in every color of the rainbow: bright red, sunny orange, even metallic blue, green, and gold. Some dragonflies have colorful stripes on their wings or bodies, and some even change color over time. What Makes an Insect a Dragonfly?
pages.brief: Several dragonflies fly with long bodies and two pairs of wings. Their colors include bright red, sunny orange, metallic blue, green, and gold. Some have colorful stripes on their wings or bodies, and some change color over time.

pages.text: Dragonflies are often confused with damselflies because the two kinds of insects resemble each other. You can tell dragonflies and damselflies apart when they land. When a damselfly isn’t flying, it folds its wings together and holds them above its back. Dragonfly wings can’t fold like a damselfly’s, so dragonflies keep their wings stretched out to either side all the time.
pages.brief: Two insects sit landed side by side. A damselfly folds its wings together and holds them above its back. A dragonfly keeps its wings stretched out to either side because its wings cannot fold like the damselfly's.

pages.text: Young Dragonflies Dragonflies need water during every stage of their life cycle. Adults lay their eggs in water or on plants near water, and the young dragonflies, called nymphs, live in water for one or more years after hatching.
pages.brief: Dragonflies need water during every stage of life. An adult dragonfly lays eggs in water or on plants near the water. Below the surface, young dragonflies called nymphs live in the water for one or more years after hatching.

pages.text: Nymphs look very different from adult dragonflies. They have gills inside their bodies, which allow them to breathe underwater. Dull green or brown coloring helps them hide from predators such as fish and frogs. To escape predators, nymphs squirt a powerful stream of water through their gills, launching themselves forward at high speed. As nymphs grow, their skin doesn’t grow with them. Instead, dragonfly nymphs shed their entire outer layer each time they need to grow. When a nymph is ready to become an adult, it crawls out of the water, and then the adult dragonfly comes out of the last shed layer.
pages.brief: Underwater, a dull green nymph hides among plants near a fish and a frog. It squirts a stream of water through its gills to launch forward, then sheds its outer layer. Later, a nymph crawls out of the water and an adult dragonfly emerges.

pages.text: Super Sight Dragonflies have amazing eyesight. Each eye is made up of about thirty thousand tiny sections. As adults, dragonflies have the largest eyes of any kind of insect. They can see in almost all directions at once, and this super eyesight helps them catch prey. They can find a single target, even in a swarm of thousands.
pages.brief: A close view shows a dragonfly's huge eyes, each made of about thirty thousand tiny sections. The dragonfly can see in almost all directions at once and focuses on a single target inside a swarm of thousands of small insects.

pages.text: Tracking Dragonflies How do scientists find out where a dragonfly swarm is headed? They glue miniature radio transmitters onto dragonflies’ bodies and then use cars and an airplane to track the dragonflies as they move across the country. Amazing Flight Adult dragonflies are among the world’s fastest flying insects, reaching speeds of one hundred body lengths per second. That’s more than 22 miles (36 km) per hour for a large dragonfly. When a dragonfly zips into high speed, it speeds up faster than the world’s fastest race cars! Male dragonflies defend their homes against other males. If they spot an intruder, they “fight” by performing high-speed flight displays. These contests let dragonflies show off their speed and size without being hurt.
pages.brief: Scientists glue a miniature radio transmitter onto a dragonfly, then track it from cars and an airplane as it crosses the country. A large dragonfly zips at high speed, faster than a race car, while two males perform a high-speed flight display to defend their homes.

pages.text: Unlike most flying insects, dragonflies control each wing independently. They can hover like helicopters or swoop and dive like fighter jets. They can fly forward, backward, and even upside down. Do You Know? Scientists study dragonfly flight in order to understand how to improve the designs of airplanes and helicopters. Scientists even hope to create a robotic dragonfly that they can send into places too tricky or dangerous for humans to visit.
pages.brief: Scientists watch a dragonfly hover, swoop, and fly upside down, studying how it controls each wing independently. Its moves are compared to a helicopter and a fighter jet. Scientists hope to improve airplanes and create a robotic dragonfly for dangerous places.

pages.text: Amazing Hunters An adult dragonfly is a high-speed flying predator, one of the most successful hunters in the animal world. Scientists say that a dragonfly catches its prey more than nine times out of ten. Compare that to a lion, which catches its dinner only one out of four attempts. Dragonflies can deliver rapid, powerful bites. They surprise mosquitoes and other small insects by attacking from behind and below. They often eat their catch without bothering to land.
pages.brief: An adult dragonfly attacks a mosquito from behind and below in midair, delivering a rapid, powerful bite and eating its catch without landing. In the background, a lion chases its dinner, showing the dragonfly is an even more successful hunter.

pages.text: Dragonflies for Dinner Dragonflies’ flying skills help them avoid most predators. Many animals like to eat dragonflies—birds, lizards, frogs, spiders, and even other dragonflies. However, not many can catch these speedy insects. Humans eat dragonflies, too. In many parts of the world, dragonflies are a special treat. You can buy them threaded onto sticks like skinny corn dogs.
pages.brief: A dragonfly zips away from a bird, lizard, frog, spider, and another dragonfly. Nearby, a person holds a stick threaded with dragonflies, like a skinny corn dog, showing that humans eat them as a special treat in many parts of the world.

pages.text: Swarms Sometimes dragonflies gather in huge groups, or swarms. They may swarm to feed on large numbers of insect prey found in one place. They also swarm to migrate south as the weather cools, the way birds travel south for the winter.
pages.brief: A huge swarm of dragonflies fills the sky, gathering where large numbers of small insect prey are found in one place. As the weather cools, the swarm moves south like migrating birds, traveling together for the winter.

pages.text: A Safe Place for Dragonflies In 1985, people in Japan created the world’s first dragonfly park. Since then, dragonfly parks have sprung up in Europe and the United States as well. Dragonflies are amazing creatures— and people all over the world are starting to realize it! Dragonflies Worldwide There are nearly three thousand kinds of dragonflies found all around the world, in almost every kind of habitat. Check out a nearby stream, pond, or lake, and see if you can spot these fancy fliers for yourself!
pages.brief: In Japan, people visit the world's first dragonfly park, created in 1985, with ponds and dragonflies flying around. Other dragonfly parks have opened in Europe and the United States. Nearly three thousand kinds live worldwide, and people can spot them near streams, ponds, and lakes.

books.title: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders
books.art_why: Yellowstone is a real place today, so photos suit its animals, geysers, and landscapes.

pages.text: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders.
pages.brief: A wide, inviting view of Yellowstone's natural landscape, with open land, scattered trees, and distant hills under a bright sky, suggesting a place full of wild wonders for visitors to explore and enjoy. The scene feels calm and open.

pages.text: Steamboat Geyser bison hot spring Introduction Imagine a place where streams of hot water shoot out of the ground and into the air. Imagine a place with beautiful green pools and bubbling pots of mud that smell like rotten eggs. Imagine a place where you can see grizzly bears, bison, and wolves in a single day.
pages.brief: A tall geyser shoots hot water and steam high into the air. Nearby, a bison stands near a bright hot spring with green pools, while bubbling mud pots send up steam. Grizzly bears and wolves appear in the distance, all within one wild place.

pages.text: Such a place is real, and it’s called Yellowstone National Park. National parks are areas of special, protected land. Yellowstone is located where Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho meet. It became the world’s first national park in 1872. Every year, millions of people visit to see its wonders.
pages.brief: A wide view of Yellowstone National Park's protected land, with mountains, forests, and open valleys. Three state regions meet at a shared boundary, and many visitors gather to see the park's natural wonders. The scene shows the park as a special place protected for everyone.

pages.text: A Hot Spot Most everyone who goes to Yellowstone wants to see Old Faithful geyser. A geyser is a hole in the ground that shoots steam and hot water into the air. Old Faithful was given its name because it will spray about every ninety minutes every day. It shoots water 100 feet (30 m) high! Yellowstone Supervolcano Yellowstone is home to an old collapsed volcano. Over the past two million years, the volcano has had three big eruptions. The rim of the collapsed volcano is huge. It is more than 45 miles (72 km) across in some places. People still watch Yellowstone closely. The volcano doesn’t look as if it is going to erupt again soon.
pages.brief: Old Faithful geyser shoots steam and hot water 100 feet into the air while a crowd of visitors watches. Beyond, the huge rim of an old collapsed volcano stretches across the landscape. People observe the area closely, though the volcano does not look likely to erupt soon.

pages.text: Yellowstone is on top of something rare called a hot spot. Heat from Earth’s core makes rocks under the ground super-hot. Rain seeps into the ground with the rocks and heats up. The hot water and steam travel up through cracks in the ground. Finally, water and steam erupt at the surface. Old Faithful is one of about three hundred geysers in Yellowstone. The hot spot has also created hot pools of bubbling mud and thousands of colorful hot springs.
pages.brief: Steam rises from cracks in the ground at Yellowstone, where a rare hot spot heats underground rocks. Rainwater seeps into the ground and becomes hot, then rises as steam and hot water. Old Faithful erupts nearby, along with bubbling mud pots and thousands of colorful hot springs.

pages.text: Wildlife When people go to Yellowstone, they also see animals of all shapes and sizes. The biggest animals in Yellowstone are bison, which can weigh up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg). They are giant animals with brown fur, a big head, and a hump on their back. In the summer, you might see them rolling in the dust to fight off flies and shed their old fur.
pages.brief: A large bison with brown fur, a big head, and a hump on its back stands in Yellowstone. In the summer heat, it rolls in the dust to fight off flies and shed its old fur. Other animals of different shapes and sizes can be seen in the park.

pages.text: The next-biggest animals are grizzly bears. They can weigh up to 800 pounds (363 kg) and are fast for their size. Grizzly bears sleep in dens underground for many months during the winter. They get up in the spring, hungry for food.
pages.brief: A grizzly bear, large and fast for its size, stands in Yellowstone. It can weigh up to 800 pounds. In winter, it sleeps in an underground den for many months. In spring, the bear wakes up and comes out hungry for food.

pages.text: Yellowstone is also home to wolves. Settlers drove wolves out of Yellowstone more than one hundred years ago. Later, workers for the national parks brought them back. Today, about one hundred wolves live in Yellowstone.
pages.brief: A pack of wolves moves through Yellowstone. Long ago, settlers drove wolves out of the park, and later park workers brought them back. Today, about one hundred wolves live here, roaming the wild land again.

pages.text: The park is also home to more than 350 other kinds of animals. Elk, deer, golden eagles, beavers, and foxes roam freely in the park. Yellowstone is a safe haven for these wild animals. Visitors can enjoy watching them but should never get too close.
pages.brief: Elk, deer, golden eagles, beavers, and foxes roam freely through Yellowstone, which is a safe haven for more than 350 other kinds of animals. Visitors watch the wild animals from a safe distance, enjoying them without getting too close.

pages.text: History Yellowstone is one of the most popular national parks in the United States. Before it became a national park, it was a place where Native peoples would hunt, fish, and gather plants. The geysers were also important to their faith.
pages.brief: Native peoples hunt, fish, and gather plants in the Yellowstone area before it becomes a national park. The geysers are important to their faith, and people gather near the steaming water. Yellowstone is one of the most popular national parks in the United States.

pages.text: Explorers also traveled through Yellowstone. They took note of its wonders through reports, photos, and paintings. Later, the United States took land where Native peoples had lived to create Yellowstone. They made laws so no one could own the land. Yellowstone was set aside for the use of many people and to take care of its animals. The idea of the national park was born.
pages.brief: Explorers travel through Yellowstone and record its wonders with reports, photos, and paintings. Later, the United States takes land where Native peoples had lived to create the park. Laws are made so no one can own the land, and Yellowstone is set aside for many people and for caring for its animals.

pages.text: There are now more than fifty national parks in the United States and many more around the world. Some, such as Grand Canyon National Park, protect natural wonders. Others, such as battlefields, protect places that are important to remember.
pages.brief: More than fifty national parks now exist in the United States, with many more around the world. Grand Canyon National Park protects a vast natural wonder, while a battlefield protects a place important to remember. Different parks set aside land for natural beauty and for history.

pages.text: Conclusion Today, about three million people from around the world travel through Yellowstone every year. They come to fish, hike, camp, watch animals, and visit the hot springs. In Yellowstone, people can see wonders rarely found anywhere else. Many people and groups help protect this special area. Yellowstone will continue to be a beautiful place to visit.
pages.brief: About three million people from around the world travel through Yellowstone each year. They fish, hike, camp, watch animals, and visit the hot springs. Many people and groups help protect this special area, so Yellowstone can continue to be a beautiful place to visit.

books.title: The Butterfly Life Cycle
books.art_why: Butterflies and their life stages are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Butterfly Life Cycle.
pages.brief: A single butterfly rests with its wings held up, shown as the main image for a book about its life cycle. The butterfly is the focus, with no other stage of the life cycle around it.

pages.text: Life Cycle of a Butterfly caterpillar pupa egg adult butterfly The Life Cycle The life cycle of a monarch butterfly consists of four stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult. A butterfly’s body transforms at each stage in its development.
pages.brief: The life cycle of a monarch butterfly is shown as four stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult butterfly. A butterfly’s body transforms at each stage in its development, moving from a tiny egg to a caterpillar, then a pupa, and finally an adult.

pages.text: Egg A female monarch butterfly lays an oval-shaped egg on the underside of a leaf. She might lay several hundred eggs in her lifetime. A caterpillar, or larva, grows inside the minuscule egg and hatches in three to twelve days.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly rests on the underside of a leaf and lays an oval-shaped egg. The oval-shaped egg is attached there. Inside the minuscule egg, a tiny caterpillar grows and hatches after three to twelve days.

pages.text: The hungry caterpillar devours food constantly because it needs a lot of food to grow. First, the caterpillar eats its own eggshell as well as any other eggs on the same leaf. Then, the caterpillar gobbles down the leaf it is resting on.
pages.brief: A hungry caterpillar on a leaf eats constantly. It first nibbles its own eggshell and other eggs on the same leaf, then gobbles down the leaf it is resting on, needing a lot of food to grow.

pages.text: The caterpillar’s body grows quickly, but its skin does not grow simultaneously. The caterpillar’s old skin splits and peels away in a process called molting, which happens many times in this stage of its life cycle. The time between each molting is called an instar.
pages.brief: A caterpillar’s body grows quickly, but its skin does not grow at the same time. The old skin splits and peels away as the caterpillar molts. This happens many times during this stage, with each period between moltings called an instar.

pages.text: Do You Know? Monarch caterpillars only eat the leaves of the milkweed plant. The new skin that is under the old skin is soft at first but soon hardens. The caterpillar molts four to six times and eats the old skin each time. The caterpillar undergoes rapid growth for two to four weeks. The more it eats, the more it can increase in size after each molting.
pages.brief: A monarch caterpillar feeds on milkweed leaves. After it molts, its new skin is soft at first and soon hardens. The caterpillar molts four to six times and eats the old skin each time, growing rapidly over two to four weeks and increasing in size after each molt.

pages.text: Pupa When the caterpillar is fully grown, it hangs upside down from a branch to prepare for the biggest change of all. It molts one last time, and this time its new skin is bright green and resembles a leaf.
pages.brief: A fully grown caterpillar hangs upside down from a branch, preparing for its biggest change. It molts one last time. Its new skin is bright green and looks like a leaf. The caterpillar stays attached to the branch as it begins this final molt.

pages.text: This green skin hardens around the caterpillar to protect it from predators as it transforms inside. The caterpillar becomes a pupa, or chrysalis (KRI-suh-lus). It will stay protected inside its shell for one to two weeks and during this time, its body is completely transformed.
pages.brief: The bright green skin hardens around the caterpillar and protects it from predators while it transforms inside. The caterpillar becomes a pupa, or chrysalis, and stays protected inside its shell for one to two weeks as its body is completely transformed.

pages.text: Adult Butterfly An adult butterfly emerges from the shell with its wet wings folded tightly against its damp body.
pages.brief: An adult butterfly emerges from the shell with its wet wings folded tightly against its damp body. The butterfly is shown just after coming out of the shell, with its wings held close to its damp body.

pages.text: The butterfly must hang upside down to rest and gain strength, or it will be unable to fly. Blood pumping into the wings causes them to unfold and spread out.
pages.brief: The butterfly hangs upside down to rest and gain strength; without this rest it will be unable to fly. Blood pumping into the wings causes them to unfold and spread out. The butterfly remains hanging as its wings open.

pages.text: The butterfly hangs for several hours while the sun and air dry its delicate wings. A butterfly has two pairs of wings that are covered in scales. The wings in the front often have a slightly different pattern from the pair in the back, but the colors on the wings are often similar to each other. When a butterfly rests, it holds its wings up.
pages.brief: The butterfly hangs for several hours while the sun and air dry its delicate wings. It has two pairs of wings covered in scales; the front and back pairs often have slightly different patterns but similar colors. When it rests, it holds its wings up.

pages.text: Once the butterfly is able to fly, it flies off to search for a mate and sustenance. Unlike a caterpillar, a butterfly does not consume leaves, but instead sips nectar from flowers with its long tongue.
pages.brief: Once the butterfly is able to fly, it flies off to search for a mate and sustenance. Unlike a caterpillar, it does not consume leaves. Instead, it sips nectar from flowers with its long tongue.

pages.text: Adult butterflies conserve their energy for flying and laying eggs instead of using it to grow. Females are usually bigger than males and have wider stripes on their wings. The last monarchs of the season will migrate, or move, to a warmer place in the late summer. These few butterflies will survive the winter until they can return home and find a mate. A monarch butterfly usually lives for two to six weeks. After she finds a mate, the female lays her eggs and starts the butterfly life cycle all over again.
pages.brief: Adult butterflies conserve energy for flying and laying eggs instead of growth. Females are usually bigger than males and have wider wing stripes. The last monarchs of the season migrate to a warmer place; a few survive winter, return home, find a mate, and the female lays eggs to start the cycle again. A monarch lives two to six weeks.

books.title: Morocco
books.art_why: Morocco is a real country today; its cities, people, animals and landforms can all be photographed.

pages.text: Morocco SPAIN Strait of Gibraltar ATLANTIC OCEAN MOROCCO Canary Islands (Spain) ALGERIA WESTERN SAHARA EUROPE ASIA MAURITANIA AFRICA Where Is It? Morocco is a country that is just a little smaller than the country of Spain. It is in northwestern Africa and has coasts along the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: A wide satellite-style view of northwestern Africa: Morocco's green and tan land lying between the deep blue Atlantic Ocean to the west and the Mediterranean Sea to the north. The narrow Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco from Spain, and pale desert sand stretches away to the south.

pages.text: The capital of Morocco is Rabat. The city is more than eight hundred years old. From the 1600s to the 1800s, Rabat was home to pirates. The pirates sailed from North Africa to raid European countries.
pages.brief: The old capital city of Rabat beside its river, with ancient stone walls and towers more than eight hundred years old. Down in the harbour, sailing ships of the kind pirates once used ride at anchor, the same ships that sailed from North Africa to raid European coasts.

pages.text: People About two-thirds of the people in Morocco live in cities. People in the cities like seeing movies, going out to eat, shopping, and going to the beach. Men like to get together in cafés to watch soccer matches on TV.
pages.brief: City life in Morocco: people filing into a cinema, families eating at outdoor restaurant tables, shoppers browsing market stalls, and bathers on a beach. In a café, men sit together over glasses of tea, eyes on a television showing a soccer match.

pages.text: About one-third of the people are farmers. Morocco has mild weather, so farmers who have enough water can grow crops easily. Religion is important in Morocco, and almost all of the people are Muslim. People mainly speak Arabic and Berber.
pages.brief: Farmers working green crop fields under mild skies, watering rows of vegetables. Nearby, worshippers gather at a mosque, and two people talk together in Arabic and in Berber, the languages most people in Morocco speak.

pages.text: Morocco’s Landforms ATLANTIC OCEAN Rabat Mount Toubkal Land Morocco has many snowy mountains. It also has forests, streams, and even waterfalls on its lands. It is home to part of the Sahara Desert as well. In the desert, few plants live except those that grow near an oasis.
pages.brief: Morocco's landforms in one sweeping view: snow-capped mountains including Mount Toubkal, dark forests, running streams and a waterfall. Beyond them the Sahara Desert rolls away in dunes, with a small oasis of palm trees and plants clustered around water.

pages.text: The weather along the coast is mild. However, in other areas it gets quite hot in the summer and quite cold in the winter.
pages.brief: Two contrasting weather scenes: a mild, breezy coastline where people walk comfortably along the shore, and inland country where summer sun beats down on cracked, dusty ground, while in winter the same inland slopes lie cold under frost and grey skies.

pages.text: History A Muslim king founded Morocco more than twelve hundred years ago. In the 1800s, Spain and France took control of it. Morocco became a free country once again in 1956. Today, Morocco has a king and a prime minister.
pages.brief: A very old mosque and city gate from the time a Muslim king founded Morocco more than twelve hundred years ago. In the foreground today, a king and a prime minister stand together outside a government building as the national flag is raised.

pages.text: Animals There are interesting animals in Morocco. M any kinds of birds live there. Ducks, storks, and other birds travel to Morocco in the winter. Camels, though, are the most famous animals in the country. Visitors can take camel rides through Morocco.
pages.brief: Wildlife across Morocco: ducks and long-legged storks with other migrating birds settling on winter wetlands, and in sandy desert country a line of camels carrying visitors on a ride, their long shadows stretching over the dunes.

pages.text: Morocco also has a kind of monkey called the Barbary macaque (muh-KAK). The Barbary macaque lives in the forests. Foxes live in the desert. They are the smallest foxes on earth. They sleep during the day and are active at night.
pages.brief: A Barbary macaque with thick brown fur sits among forest branches. Out in the desert, the tiny fennec fox with huge ears curls asleep in a shady den by day, then stands alert and bright-eyed on the sand at night.

pages.text: Food Many people from around the world love the food of Morocco. People in Morocco often eat a tiny round pasta called couscous. They also eat most kinds of meat. One dish is a flaky crust filled with meat. It is topped with sugar. Some people in Morocco like to drink a sweet mint tea with their meals.
pages.brief: A Moroccan meal spread out: a mound of tiny round couscous pasta, plates of meat, and a flaky pastry pie filled with meat and dusted with sugar on top. Beside the dishes, a glass of sweet mint tea is being poured.

pages.text: Conclusion Morocco has snowy mountains, green fields, golden sand dunes, and nice beaches. Morocco is home to many interesting people and animals. Its food is famous all around the world. Morocco is an ancient and beautiful country.
pages.brief: A last look across Morocco: snow-tipped mountains behind green fields, golden sand dunes, and a curve of pale beach meeting blue water. People go about their day and animals graze as the country's varied landscapes stretch from horizon to horizon.

pages.text: Morocco Population: 33,322,699 Land: 446,300 square kilometers (172,317 sq. mi.) Capital City: Rabat Primary Languages: Arabic, Berber Primary Religion: Islam Name of Currency: dirham.
pages.brief: A broad view of the capital Rabat beside the Atlantic, with farmland and distant mountains behind it, and people walking its streets carrying dirham coins. The scene stands for the country the numbers describe: its people, its capital, its languages and its faith.

books.title: 1849: The California Gold Rush
books.art_why: The book covers 1849 historical events that cannot be shown in real photographs, so drawings fit.

pages.text: 1849: The California Gold Rush.
pages.brief: A broad historical view of California's gold country in 1849, with a river, hills, and a miner's pan resting near the water, suggesting the time, place, and subject of the California Gold Rush for young readers.

pages.text: Keeping a Secret On the morning of January 24, 1848, James Marshall was working at a mill in California. He spotted something shiny under the water in a ditch. It was gold! Marshall showed the gold to the owner of the mill, John Sutter. Sutter tried to get everyone to keep the secret that gold had been found. Six days later, California became part of the United States.
pages.brief: James Marshall kneels at a mill beside a ditch and spots shiny gold under the water. He shows the gold to John Sutter, the mill owner. Sutter speaks to everyone, trying to keep the discovery secret.

pages.text: Territory Lost to the U.S. in the Mexican-American War United States Mexico Sam Brannan, who owned a store on Sutter’s land, soon let out the secret. He sold miners the tools they needed to find gold (picks, axes, pans, and shovels)—at very high prices. John Sutter John Sutter moved to California from Switzerland. Mexico controlled California at the time. Sutter made a deal with the Mexican government to control a large amount of land that actually belonged to Native peoples. Sutter made some Native people part of his own army. He enslaved many others to work the land.
pages.brief: A map shows territory Mexico lost to the United States. Sam Brannan sells picks, axes, pans, and shovels to miners at high prices. John Sutter stands over large land, with Native people forced into his army or enslaved to work it.

pages.text: Panning Unlike gold in most places, California’s gold wasn’t locked deep under the ground. Placer mining was a way that miners sifted gold out of the riverbed using a shallow, flat pan. Prospectors stood in rivers and shoveled gravel into their pan. They took out large rocks, then carefully swirled the pan. The dirt and gravel spilled over the edges with the water. The shiny flakes of gold stayed at the bottom of the pan. Word Wise A prospector is someone who moves to a spot with the prospect, or possibility, of finding gold.
pages.brief: Prospectors stand in a river and shovel gravel into shallow, flat pans. They remove large rocks and swirl the pans carefully, letting dirt and gravel spill out with the water while shiny flakes of gold stay at the bottom.

pages.text: The Forty-Niners Gold fever— greed and excitement brought on by the discovery of gold— took hold of many people. At the time, many workers earned less than a dollar a day. In 1849, around ninety thousand people—called forty- niners —joined the Gold Rush. People from Mexico and countries in Central and South America traveled to California. Some enslaved Black people were brought by their enslavers. Free Black people also came. The trip to the gold mines could take months—and was not cheap. People had to pay to get there and for food during travel. Many forty-niners planned to make money quickly and return home. Others were ready for adventure.
pages.brief: Many people travel toward California during the Gold Rush, called forty-niners. Workers who earned less than a dollar a day join the crowd. People come from Mexico, Central America, South America, and elsewhere; some enslaved Black people are brought, and free Black people come too.

pages.text: People from California, Oregon, and Mexico were the first to come to the rivers near Sutter’s Mill. Locals only had to take their pack animals. It took longer for immigrants to arrive by boat. They came from Asia, Australia, and South America. By Ship About half of the forty-niners decided to travel by ship to avoid crossing the lands of Native peoples. Ships took from five to eight months to sail from the East Coast. They had to round the tip of South America and then go up the coast to California. The cheapest ticket was $75—about $2,300 today. It was a difficult journey. People got sick and were bored.
pages.brief: Near Sutter's Mill, people from California, Oregon, and Mexico arrive first with pack animals. Later, immigrants come by ship from Asia, Australia, and South America. A ship rounds the tip of South America, carrying bored and sick passengers on the long, costly journey to California.

pages.text: The Routes the Forty-Niners Took NORTH AMERICA PACIFIC OCEAN KEY Overland route (five to eight months) ATLANTIC OCEAN SOUTH AMERICA.
pages.brief: A map of North America, South America, the Pacific Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean presents two long routes taken by forty-niners: an overland route across the continent and a sea route around the southern tip of South America.

pages.text: Some passengers cut through Panama. They traveled across 60 miles (97 km) of jungle, then got on another ship. Bad weather and wild animals made the shortcut difficult. Many fell ill and died. If they made it across, it might take weeks or months to catch a ship on the other side. By Wagon It took about the same amount of time to cross the United States by wagon. Much of the land between forty-niners on the East Coast and California still belonged to Native peoples. Settlers moving West often stole from Native communities and attacked them.
pages.brief: Travelers cut through sixty miles of Panama jungle, facing bad weather and wild animals; many fall ill or die while waiting for another ship. Elsewhere, wagon settlers cross land that belongs to Native peoples, and settlers often steal from Native communities and attack them.

pages.text: Most people left from St. Louis, Missouri, the most western U.S. city at the time. Wagons followed the California Trail for 2,100 miles (3,380 km) across the flat prairie. A wagon could travel about 15 miles (24 km) in a day. Rivers, mountains, cliffs, and deserts greeted the travelers, as well as rain, wind, and snow. It was difficult to keep the oxen healthy and the wagons working. Even worse dangers facing forty-niners came from sicknesses, hunger, and accidents. For those who made it to California, life did not get easier. Still, it was difficult for miners to give up—the next pan of gravel might have gold!
pages.brief: A wagon train leaves St. Louis, Missouri, following the California Trail for 2,100 miles across flat prairie. Oxen pull wagons past rivers, mountains, cliffs, and deserts through rain, wind, and snow. Sickness, hunger, and accidents threaten the travelers.

pages.text: Equal Opportunity? As the hills filled with prospectors, white miners began to treat other groups badly. Many different groups of Native peoples lived in California. Attacks from forty-niners forced Native peoples off their land. Once California became a state in 1850, the government took even more land from Native peoples. Thousands of Native peoples were killed and thousands more died of sickness. New laws allowed settlers to arrest Native people for breaking the law. They then forced them to pay fines by working on ranches. White prospectors wanted as little competition as possible. California forced miners from other countries to leave by taxing them, including those from China.
pages.brief: White prospectors crowd the hills and treat other groups badly, forcing Native peoples off their land. Native people are arrested, fined, and forced to work on ranches. Miners from China and other countries are taxed and pushed to leave California.

pages.text: Finding gold wasn’t easy. Even those who found gold often lost it. Robbers were common. Goods cost a lot of money. Some early prospectors got rich. Mostly large companies could mine for the deeper gold, so they were the most successful. Prices Gone Wild.
pages.brief: Miners search for gold, though finding it is hard and robbers are common. Goods cost a lot of money. Some early prospectors get rich, while large companies succeed most by mining deeper gold. Prices rise wildly around the goldfields.

pages.text: Some people got rich just by selling goods to the miners. Sam Brannan became one of the first millionaires in the United States. Levi Strauss sold pants tough enough to handle the work—blue jeans. Women started businesses cooking, running boarding houses, and washing clothes. Mary Ellen Pleasant Mary Ellen Pleasant was a Black American businesswoman who worked as a cook and a housekeeper during the Gold Rush. While she worked, she listened to what businesspeople were talking about. Pleasant became a millionaire buying and selling buildings and businesses.
pages.brief: Sam Brannan sells goods to miners and becomes a millionaire. Levi Strauss sells tough pants that become blue jeans. Women run cooking, boarding house, and laundry businesses. Mary Ellen Pleasant, a Black businesswoman, works as a cook and housekeeper, listens to businesspeople, and buys and sells buildings and businesses.

pages.text: The Golden State The Gold Rush brought success to white settlers, the U.S. government, and rich people. Unfortunately, the Gold Rush was also harmful in many ways. It brought around three hundred thousand settlers, mostly white, to what were once Native lands in California. More than one hundred thousand Native peoples were dead twenty years after the Gold Rush had begun. The Gold Rush forever changed the western United States. Today, California has more people than any of the other forty-nine states. Nearly two centuries after the Gold Rush, California still lives up to its nickname: the Golden State.
pages.brief: California today is crowded, with more people than any other state, still called the Golden State. The Gold Rush brought success to white settlers and rich people, but it also brought three hundred thousand settlers to Native lands and left more than one hundred thousand Native peoples dead.

books.title: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park
books.art_why: The book covers eruptions and park history from the 1700s and 1800s, when photos of these events were impossible.

pages.text: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park PACIFIC OCEAN A Volcano Wonderland Every day on the island of Hawaii, lava seeps from a volcano on the edge of the ocean. When the lava cools, it turns into rock and makes the island a little bigger. This volcano is part of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Every year, over one million people visit Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. National parks are areas of protected land.
pages.brief: On the island of Hawaii, a volcano at the edge of the Pacific Ocean sends lava seeping toward the water. Cooled lava has turned into black rock, extending the island’s edge. In the distance, a small group of visitors stands in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, a protected area.

pages.text: Volcanoes Form a Park A volcano begins when melted rock from deep inside Earth comes out through a crack in Earth’s surface. When it reaches the surface, it cools and becomes solid rock. The rock builds up over time. The rock may form a mountain or even an island. This is how Hawaii’s islands formed. Two of the world’s most amazing volcanoes are found in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Inside a Volcano.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows melted rock deep inside Earth rising through a crack to a volcano’s surface. The rock cools and builds into solid layers that form a mountain and an island. Two great volcanoes stand within Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.

pages.text: One volcano is among the most active volcanoes on Earth. Scientists think it began forming between 300,000 and 600,000 years ago. It finally formed as an island 50,000 to 100,000 years ago.
pages.brief: A broad, active volcano rises from the ocean, with dark lava flows across its slopes. Two scientists stand at a distance, looking toward the mountain. The scene shows the volcano as it formed over hundreds of thousands of years and became an island.

pages.text: In 1790, dozens of people were killed when it erupted. Then, in 1924, more eruptions threw huge rocks around the area. Leaping Lava In 1959, one volcano sent a stream of lava 1,900 feet (579 m) into the air— about twice the height of the Eiffel Tower!
pages.brief: A volcano erupts violently, sending a towering fountain of lava high into the air and throwing huge rocks across the slopes. Near the base, a few people from long ago stand at a distance. The glowing lava column is far taller than the surrounding land.

pages.text: Nearby is another volcano that is one of the biggest mountains on Earth. It covers half the island of Hawaii. This volcano has erupted many times since 1843.
pages.brief: A vast, gently sloping volcano dominates the island of Hawaii, covering half the land in dark lava flows. It is one of the biggest mountains on Earth. Its broad summit and long slopes stretch toward the ocean, with older eruptions visible in the rocky layers.

pages.text: In 1868, an eruption caused earthquakes that lasted four days and destroyed nearly forty buildings.
pages.brief: A small town near the volcano is shaken by strong earthquakes. Cracks open in the ground, and nearly forty buildings are damaged or destroyed. The scene shows the four days of shaking caused by an 1868 eruption.

pages.text: An Amazing History People have been visiting the volcanoes for hundreds of years.
pages.brief: For hundreds of years, people have traveled to the volcanoes. A group of visitors stands on a rocky overlook, gazing across a wide volcanic landscape. Their presence shows a long history of people coming to see the amazing volcanoes.

pages.text: They wanted to protect both the volcanoes and the land around them. The area was named a national park in 1916.
pages.brief: People gather near the volcano to protect the land around it. The broad landscape includes volcanic slopes and open ground. The scene shows the protected area as it was named a national park in 1916, with the volcanoes and surrounding land kept safe for the future.

pages.text: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is 520 square miles (1,347 sq km). It has volcanoes and lava tubes that flow to the sea. Lava tubes are big tunnels in the ground. They are so big that people can walk through them.
pages.brief: A wide view shows the national park with volcanoes and long lava tubes running toward the sea. Inside one lava tube, a large tunnel stretches far ahead, big enough for people to walk through. The park covers 520 square miles of volcanic landscape.

pages.text: Wildlife at the Volcanoes’ Edge Hundreds of protected animals live in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. The park is home to turtles, bats, insects, and many types of birds.
pages.brief: At the edge of the volcanoes, protected wildlife lives among the rocks and plants. A sea turtle rests near the shore, a bat hangs in a sheltered spot, insects cling to leaves, and several kinds of birds perch nearby. Hundreds of protected animals make their home in the park.

pages.text: The park also has many protected plants and trees. Almost all of its plants are found only in Hawaii. Many plants have lived in and around the volcanoes for years.
pages.brief: Many protected plants and trees grow on the volcanic slopes. Almost all of them are found only in Hawaii, and many have lived in and around the volcanoes for years. Green leaves and branches rise from rocky ground, showing the park’s special plant life.

pages.text: Enjoy—But Watch Your Step! Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is a wonderful place to visit. Drive along a volcano or hike more than 150 miles (241 km) of trails. Bike along the volcano’s paths or camp in the rainforest. It’s almost impossible to know when a volcano will erupt. However, when eruptions are possible, parts of the park close. This special park is never quiet for long.
pages.brief: Visitors enjoy the park in different ways: one person drives along a volcano road, others hike a trail, a cyclist rides a path, and a tent sits in the rainforest. Nearby, a volcano sends up a plume, showing that eruptions can happen and parts of the park may close.

books.title: Amazing Antarctica
books.art_why: The book includes 1820 exploration and discovery, so drawn scenes suit the historical pages.

pages.text: Amazing Antarctica.
pages.brief: A wide view of Antarctica’s frozen landscape, with vast white ice sheets and a rugged icy coastline under a pale sky. The remote southern continent stretches out immense and empty, with no people in sight.

pages.text: The Seven Continents 1 North America 2 South America The Seventh Continent On it you can easily find six continents: Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. These lands have been home to humans for many thousands of years. Now look at the bottom of the globe. There you will find continent number seven: Antarctica.
pages.brief: A globe of Earth shows Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America spread across the world, with Antarctica at the bottom. The six inhabited continents sit above the seventh frozen continent far below.

pages.text: Antarctica is located far from where anyone lives. It is surrounded by rough seas. For a long time, no one knew it was there. Many explorers have sailed the stormy Antarctic waters throughout history. However, people didn’t actually discover Antarctica until around 1820. No one individual is given credit for its discovery. A few men are said to have sighted it within days of each other. Historians also do not agree on the first people to explore its lands.
pages.brief: A sailing ship battles rough, stormy Antarctic waters while explorers on deck search the horizon. In the distance, icy land appears faintly. Another ship is nearby, suggesting several explorers sighted the continent around 1820 within days of one another.

pages.text: Antarctica SOUTH ATLANTIC OCEAN SOUTH PACIFIC OCEAN INDIAN OCEAN Over the last two hundred years, we have learned that Antarctica is a place of extremes. It is the coldest and windiest continent. It gets the least rain and snow. Antarctica also has some of the most amazing wildlife in the world.
pages.brief: An illustrated view of Antarctica surrounded by the South Atlantic, South Pacific, and Indian Oceans. Rough blue waters ring the icy continent. Near the coast, wildlife gathers in the cold, showing Antarctica as a place of extremes.

pages.text: Freezing Antarctica During the winter, Earth’s southern half is turned away from the Sun. For a couple of weeks in June and July—winter in Antarctica—the Sun never rises. For a period in December and January—summer in Antarctica—the Sun never sets. Antarctica’s location means the weather is usually cold, icy, and windy. The temperature in summer most often reaches just above 0°C (32°F). In winter, the temperature is almost always below –18°C (0°F). The coldest temperature ever recorded on Earth was at an Antarctic science station in July 1983. It got down to –89°C (–128°F).
pages.brief: Antarctica under a dark winter sky, with the Sun hidden below the horizon while icy wind sweeps across the frozen ground. In another view, summer sunlight stays in the sky over the ice, never setting, lighting the cold white land.

pages.text: This extreme cold is why thick sheets of ice cover Antarctica. At its deepest, Antarctica’s ice is 4 kilometers (2.5 mi.) thick. With all that ice, it might seem surprising that Antarctica is also the driest continent. It gets less than 5 centimeters (2 in.) of rain and snow a year.
pages.brief: A thick sheet of ice covers Antarctica, shown as a deep layer over the land. Very little snow falls from a pale sky, emphasizing that the icy continent is also extremely dry. The ice stretches far into the distance.

pages.text: Most of Earth is covered by water. However, this water is mostly salt water. Most of Earth’s fresh water is frozen in Antarctica’s ice. Since snow doesn’t melt away during the cold Antarctic summers, ice has been building up over thousands of years.
pages.brief: Vast Antarctic ice holds most of Earth’s fresh water, frozen solid. Snow lies on top without melting through cold summers, and layer upon layer of old ice has built up over thousands of years across the continent.

pages.text: Life on and Around Antarctica The bitter weather conditions in Antarctica have made it a dangerous habitat for life to survive. The continent has no trees. Only low plants, such as moss, grow there. The continent has one native insect: the tiny Antarctic midge. Almost all plant and animal life on Antarctica is found near the coasts or in the sea. Among the creatures that call the icy Antarctic waters home is the emperor penguin, the largest penguin in the world. It stands more than 1.2 meters (4 ft.) tall.
pages.brief: A coastal Antarctic scene with low moss growing on rock, a tiny midge, and an emperor penguin standing near the sea. No trees appear; plant and animal life is gathered by the coast and in the icy water.

pages.text: Leopard seals are fast, fierce predators that hunt penguins and other prey in the open water. The second-largest kind of seal in the world, leopard seals can grow more than 3.3 meters (11 ft.) long and can weigh up to 590 kilograms (1,300 lb.). Wowser! A male emperor penguin has a big job when it comes to a baby penguin. It stands on ice and holds an egg between its feet and body for two months. The male doesn’t eat for this entire period and loses almost half its weight. If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the father stays with the chick. Once the mother comes back, she feeds fish to the chick. The father can finally go to the sea to eat.
pages.brief: A leopard seal swims fast through open water, hunting prey. On the ice, a male emperor penguin stands holding an egg between his feet and body. Nearby, a mother penguin feeds fish to a chick.

pages.text: A Playground for Scientists People around the world have worked hard to protect Antarctica’s wildlife and land. Thirty countries have about seventy research bases on Antarctica. Some are open year-round. Others are only open in summer. Do You Know? No one country has control of Antarctica. In 1961, many countries signed an agreement, called a treaty. It makes sure no wars happen in Antarctica and scientists can peacefully study there.
pages.brief: Several research bases stand on the icy Antarctic landscape, with scientists working outside among the snow. The scene suggests international cooperation, with people from many countries sharing the frozen continent peacefully for study and science.

pages.text: Some scientists come to study the wildlife—on land and in the water. For example, some scientists record what penguins eat and how they behave. Other scientists study Antarctica’s ice. They measure how it changes. They also drill down and pull out ice tubes called cores. These cores contain bubbles of air that can inform scientists about what the air in Antarctica was like long ago.
pages.brief: Scientists observe emperor penguins near the coast, recording their behavior and food. Others drill into the ice and pull out long ice cores, studying trapped air bubbles to learn what Antarctica’s air was like long ago.

pages.text: Some of Antarctica’s giant ice shelves —floating pieces of ice attached to land—have been dropping into the ocean. Scientists are studying the ice melting in Antarctica and other places. It may cause problems around the world someday. In addition to scientists, thousands of tourists visit Antarctica each year. Most arrive on ships to experience one of the most remote places on Planet Earth.
pages.brief: A giant ice shelf breaks and drops into the ocean, while scientists measure the changing ice. In the distance, a tourist ship carries visitors toward Antarctica’s remote coast, showing one of the most faraway places on Earth.

pages.text: Conclusion Antarctica remains one of the least-known lands in the world. The cold, ice, and rough seas make it a difficult place to explore and study. However, it’s a place of uncommon beauty that offers opportunities to study an extreme habitat.
pages.brief: A remote Antarctic coast under a cold sky, with rough seas crashing against ice and snow. The frozen landscape looks beautiful but harsh, a difficult place to explore and study, yet full of uncommon natural beauty.

books.title: Here Come the Locusts
books.art_why: The book covers the 1874 Great Plains plague, pioneer times and ancient history, where no photograph of the events exists.

pages.text: A Flying Plague It’s been dry for weeks on the prairie. The corn is turning brown. It needs rain. A cloud appears in the distance. At first, the farmers are hopeful, but they soon realize that something is very wrong. The sky turns brown. Then there is a sound like hail falling on the roof.
pages.brief: A wide prairie farm under a pale, dry sky, corn stalks turning brown in cracked soil. In the distance a small dark cloud grows, and farmers stand in a field looking up at it, hopeful at first, as the sky darkens to brown above the corn.

pages.text: It’s insects—millions of them—landing on every surface. They chew away the corn, the grass, the trees, and the gardens. They even eat the clothes hanging on the line. Millions of jaws make a sound like a grass fire. Then, just as suddenly, the cloud rises and disappears. The farmers have lost everything. They have just lived through a plague of locusts.
pages.brief: Millions of locusts drop onto a farmyard, covering the ground, fences, trees and a row of clothes hanging on a line. Insects swarm over chewed corn and bare branches while farmers watch helplessly, and then the brown cloud lifts away into the sky, leaving stripped fields behind.

pages.text: Locusts Throughout History All through history, people feared swarms of locusts. Millions of these large, colorful grasshoppers seemed to appear out of nowhere. They ate every plant in sight. They ate farmers’ crops. They ate grass, leaving other animals with no food. If the swarm was large enough, it could cause famine. Many ancient and religious texts talk about plagues of locusts. The swarms were often seen as a warning or punishment.
pages.brief: A great swarm of large, colorful grasshoppers sweeps across an ancient landscape, blanketing crops, grass and wild plants. In the foreground people of an early settlement stand among ruined fields, and rolled scrolls resting nearby suggest old writings that record such plagues.

pages.text: When pioneers in the United States came west in the eighteen hundreds, swarms of locusts destroyed their crops. In 1874, locusts covered the Great Plains. They ate over 5 million square kilometers (2 million sq. mi.) of crops, the wool from live sheep, and clothing off people’s backs. They even got into kitchen cupboards and ate everything inside. So many got squashed on the roads and train rails that it became too slippery to travel. The locusts destroyed millions of dollars’ worth of crops. Many families had to leave their new farms.
pages.brief: Pioneer families on the Great Plains in the 1870s stand outside their sod houses as locusts cover the fields, the sheep, the washing and the garden. Some insects cluster in an open kitchen cupboard, and crushed locusts smear the muddy road and the iron train rails.

pages.text: A Flying Mystery One of the scariest things about locusts was that no one knew where they came from. During quiet years, there were no swarms or even a single locust. Then suddenly, millions appeared without warning. Female locusts laid eggs in the soil. Then the swarm moved on. The next year, everything was quiet again. No new locusts came from the eggs.
pages.brief: A quiet, empty field of green grass with no insects in sight, then a cutaway view of soil where a female locust pushes eggs into the earth before the swarm lifts away. The eggs lie buried through a still, silent season with nothing hatching above them.

pages.text: Where did they go? When would they come back? Why? Early in the twentieth century, scientists began to look into the mystery. A scientist named Boris Uvarov studied the desert locust, a very harmful species in the Middle East. His experiments changed everything we know about locusts.
pages.brief: In an early twentieth-century laboratory, a scientist in a shirt and tie leans over glass jars and wooden cages holding desert locusts brought from the Middle East. Notebooks and simple instruments sit on the bench as he studies the insects closely.

pages.text: A Strange Change Uvarov found that desert locust eggs did not hatch into baby locusts. Instead, they became short-horned grasshoppers. They were smaller and duller in color than their locust parents. They also acted quite differently. They did not form swarms that flew from place to place. Short-horned grasshoppers lived alone. They avoided other grasshoppers. Each grasshopper stayed in one small area. They never caused much damage. So where did locusts come from? Uvarov did more experiments. When he forced the short-horned grasshoppers to live close together, something shocking happened.
pages.brief: The scientist watches small, dull-colored short-horned grasshoppers in a cage, each one sitting apart in its own patch and turning away from the others. Beside this, a crowded cage shows the same grasshoppers packed tightly together, bumping into one another.

pages.text: If grasshoppers kept bumping into their neighbors, they changed color. Instead of avoiding each other, they joined a group. Together, the grasshoppers formed swarms. All at once, they took to the air. The harmless grasshoppers had become locusts. Grasshopper to Locust—and Back Again.
pages.brief: Inside a crowded cage, grasshoppers jostle and bump into their neighbors, their bodies shifting from dull brown to brighter color. They gather into a tight group, then rise together into the air above the laboratory, flying off as a swarm.

pages.text: Grasshopper Locust Changing to Live Uvarov showed that some animals can change, depending on the conditions around them. The change helps them live. During a drought, the grasshoppers’ food supply shrinks. The grasshoppers follow their food. All the grasshoppers in an area end up crowded together in one spot, such as a wetland. When things get too crowded, certain types of grasshoppers change into locusts.
pages.brief: A dry, cracked landscape during a drought, with grasshoppers moving across parched ground toward a shrinking patch of green wetland. The insects crowd together at the water's edge, packed shoulder to shoulder, as their bodies begin to change into locusts.

pages.text: Together, they fly off in search of more food. They land in one place, eat everything, and then move on. Changing into locusts helps these grasshoppers get through the drought.
pages.brief: A dense swarm of locusts lifts from the wetland and flies across open country in search of food. They settle on a green field, cover it completely while chewing every plant, then rise again and move on toward the horizon.

pages.text: Controlling Locusts Locusts can still hurt farmers today. Swarms are usually found in dry areas, such as North Africa, the Middle East, and Australia. However, Uvarov’s discovery changed how people fight locusts. Before, people tried to stop swarms by spraying poison over a wide area. The poison harmed other living things, including helpful insects such as bees. Other farmers burned their crops. The fires destroyed the swarm but also the crops. Sometimes the farmers’ efforts were still not enough.
pages.brief: A farmer in a dry region of North Africa or the Middle East sprays poison across a wide field, while bees and other insects fall among the crops. Nearby, other fields burn, with fire and smoke rising from crops the farmers set alight.

pages.text: Today, people keep a close eye on grasshoppers. They watch the weather and notice when a drought begins. Weather instruments can spot swarms while they are still small. Farmers can apply little bits of poison to small areas. The poison prevents large swarms from forming. It can save millions of dollars’ worth of crops. Locusts rarely cause famines anymore. The better we understand these insects, the better we can live with them.
pages.brief: Farmers and scientists today stand at the edge of a field watching grasshoppers closely, with a weather instrument on a pole nearby. One worker applies a small dab of poison to a limited patch of ground while healthy crops stretch away under open sky.

books.title: Animal Groups: Strength in Numbers
books.art_why: Real animals and nature scenes exist in the real world.

pages.text: Animal Groups: Strength in Numbers.
pages.brief: A wide open natural landscape shows many different wild animals gathered in clusters, with large groups standing close together and a few solitary animals apart in the distance, suggesting animal groups and strength in numbers.

pages.text: Animal Groups: Animal Groups: Strength in Numbers Strength in Numbers.
pages.brief: A calm nature scene presents several kinds of wild animals arranged in separate small groups across open ground, some clustered closely and others farther apart, giving a broad view of animals living together in strength.

pages.text: Introduction Did you know that a group of giraffes is a tower? Or that a group of crows is a murder? There are also pods of whales, swarms of bees, and schools of fish. All these unique names point out something important: many animals live in groups. Yet other animals, such as tigers, moles, and sloths, live just fine all alone. So why do some animals team up, and how does each animal fit into its group?
pages.brief: A tall giraffe stands with other giraffes in a tower, crows gather in a murder, whales swim in a pod, bees swarm and fish school, while a tiger, a mole and a sloth sit alone in their own habitats.

pages.text: Small Families A small family is made up of parents and their young. For some animals, such as skunks, cheetahs, orangutans, and grizzly bears, a family is a mother that raises her babies. For others, including penguins, parrots, foxes, and finches, both mothers and fathers bring up their young. Small families often have close bonds. Mother cheetahs groom their babies by licking them. Baby bears play with each other and their parents. Crane parents dance together, seabirds call, and fox families pounce and play. These bonds encourage members of the family to care for and protect each other.
pages.brief: A mother cheetah licks her cubs while baby bears play with each other and their parents; crane parents dance together, seabirds call, and a fox family pounces and plays, showing close bonds in small animal families.

pages.text: The main job of small families is caring for the young. Some families only stay together until the young can live on their own. A mother moose and her calf stay side by side for about a year. When the calf is grown, it leaves. After that, moose live solitary lives. Other families last for the long term. Pairs of albatrosses, which are large seabirds, stick together for life. That’s saying a lot since albatrosses can live more than fifty years! Solitary Animals Some animals, such as bears, moose, and certain wildcats, do not benefit from group living. Solitary animals live alone— except when they are raising young—to avoid competing with their own kind for mates or territory.
pages.brief: A mother moose stands side by side with her calf in the wild, while a pair of albatrosses stays close together; a solitary bear and a wildcat are shown alone, avoiding competition for mates or territory.

pages.text: Animals that form small families often have helpless young. Most are birds or mammals. Bird parents must feed babies until they can fly. Baby mammals nurse from their mothers. A few other kinds of animals form small families as well. For example, mother crocodiles guard their babies from hungry fish or birds. Clown fish fathers fan fresh water over their eggs to care for them. Small families make sure the young grow big, healthy, and skilled enough to survive on their own.
pages.brief: Bird parents feed their babies until they can fly, a mother mammal nurses her young, a mother crocodile guards her babies from hungry fish and birds, and a clown fish father fans fresh water over his eggs in their habitats.

pages.text: Bands Animal families can be small or large. Some animals live in bands, or extended families. Bands include mothers, fathers, young, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, and other relatives. Some bands include unrelated animals. They are usually mates of the family members. Rarely, a band will adopt another animal that has no band. Lions, wolves, whales, dolphins, monkeys, chimps, and elephants all live in bands. Bands work together to raise young. Some adult animals watch the young while others find food. Siblings, cousins, and other youngsters all play together.
pages.brief: An elephant band includes mothers, fathers, young, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, with some adults watching the calves while others find food; lion, wolf and dolphin bands are also shown, and siblings and cousins play together.

pages.text: Bands also work together to find food. Wolves, lions, and dolphins are famous for using sophisticated teamwork to hunt prey. An elephant matriarch, often the oldest female, leads her family to remote food and water sources as they follow behind in single file. Many bands also work together to defend a territory. Life in a band can be complex. Often, one or two animals act as leaders. In some groups, such as elephant bands, leadership passes peacefully from parent to young. Chimps and monkeys, on the other hand, can be competitive over mates or territory. Followers try to take control and may flash their teeth to challenge others. They team up with other followers or even fight the leader.
