pages.brief: An elephant matriarch leads her family to food and water in single file, while wolves, lions and dolphins work together to hunt; a chimpanzee or monkey flashes its teeth to challenge a leader in a competitive band.

pages.text: Do You Know? Some of the smartest animals on Earth—dolphins, chimps, and elephants—live in bands. Some scientists think that high intelligence helps these animals keep track of complex relationships within their groups. Bands work best when members get along. Band leaders have more power when they have more support. Members of bands strengthen their bonds by grooming, playing, or relaxing together. They also communicate with sound, scent, and movement. Elephants rumble and trumpet to express themselves. Wolves and wild dogs leave scent marks as a way to claim territory and recognize each other. Groups as large as bands use behaviors like these to cooperate.
pages.brief: Elephants rumble and trumpet to communicate, chimpanzees groom and relax together, and wolves and wild dogs leave scent marks to claim territory and recognize each other in their habitats, showing how intelligent band members strengthen bonds and cooperate.

pages.text: Herds Groups even bigger than bands have learned to work together. Imagine the African savanna. Grazing animals move across the land as far as the eye can see. Herds of mammals, flocks of birds, and schools of fish are some of the largest animal groups. All of these groups, generally known as herds, take advantage of their large numbers to stay safe from predators. Lions can easily attack a single zebra. However, they have trouble picking one out of a crowd, especially when that crowd is on the run. Family Herds Some herds and flocks are made up of small families. One example is penguin colonies, in which thousands of parents raise their chicks.
pages.brief: On the African savanna, a large herd of grazing mammals moves across the land, flocks of birds and schools of fish gather in big groups, and lions try to pick one zebra out of a running crowd; a penguin colony fills the scene.

pages.text: More animals also means more eyes. If one gazelle spots a cheetah, it sounds the alarm by making a honking sound. Then the whole herd has a chance to get away. For these reasons, many animals live in herds to raise young. The large group helps protect the babies. Members of herds often communicate. In addition to using alarm calls to warn of predators, they use calls to help everyone stick together. However, unlike families and bands, herds do not form bonds. Above all else, each member of a herd looks out for itself.
pages.brief: A gazelle spots a cheetah and makes a honking alarm call, then the whole herd runs away; baby animals stay protected inside the large group, while members use calls to stick together but do not form close bonds.

pages.text: Societies It is amazing enough that groups as large as herds have figured out how to cooperate. Another kind of group, called a society, has thousands or even hundreds of thousands of individuals. Unlike herds, societies are organized. The members work together for the good of the group. Very few animals form societies, and nearly all of those that do are insects, including ants, termites, bees, and some wasps. Do You Know? The naked mole rat is one of the few noninsects to form a society. Naked mole rats have queens and workers. Some scientists also classify humans as an animal society. Unlike other societies, humans can work with others who are not related.
pages.brief: Ants, termites, bees and some wasps live in organized societies, while a naked mole rat colony has a queen and workers; nearby, humans are shown working together with others who are not related, a rare kind of animal society.

pages.text: In a society, every member has a job. Workers gather food, nurses care for the young, and soldiers protect the group. Some insect workers even have different kinds of bodies to help them do their jobs! Usually, one queen lays all the eggs. This means that every member of a society is related. Insect societies can do incredible things. Leaf- and grass-cutter ants chop up leaves, bring them into their nests, and use them to fertilize fungus farms. Bees build wax cells for their own special food—honey. Ants create scent trails to help each other find food and bring it back to the nest. Termites build mounds over 5 meters (17 ft.) tall. Considering the size of a termite, these mounds are like giant skyscrapers. Societies can do all this because everyone works together.
pages.brief: Worker ants carry cut leaves into nests for fungus farms, nurse insects care for the young, soldier insects protect the group, a queen lays eggs, bees build wax cells for honey, and termites raise tall mounds; every society member has a job.

pages.text: Conclusion Many kinds of animals live in groups, from tiny termites to enormous elephants. Groups help animals raise and protect young. They help members find food. They can even build structures together. Though groups come in different sizes and different styles, they all help animals survive.
pages.brief: Tiny termites and enormous elephants are shown in groups across different habitats, with young animals protected, food found, and structures built together; groups of many sizes and styles help animals survive, from insects to elephants.

books.title: The Everglades
books.art_why: Includes historical Indigenous peoples and 1800s events where real photos are impossible.

pages.text: Weird and Wonderful Have you ever heard of a gumbo-limbo? How about a skink or a stinkpot? These aren’t cartoon characters. They’re the names of plants and animals that live in Everglades National Park in Florida. This weird and wonderful place is unlike any other.
pages.brief: A gumbo-limbo plant, a skink, and a stinkpot are shown in Everglades National Park in Florida, a weird and wonderful place unlike any other. The scene focuses on unusual plants and animals that live in the park.

pages.text: More Than a Swamp Everglades National Park lies within the area known as the Everglades, which makes up much of South Florida. The park is only a small part of the Everglades region. The region is the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States. It has hot, wet summers and mild, dry winters. Some people may think the Everglades region is just a big wet swamp. The Everglades does have a great deal of water, but its waters connect different ecosystems. Each of these ecosystems supports different life-forms. Many of the mammals, reptiles, birds, and fish are only found in the Everglades. Where Are the Everglades? KEY Georgia Alabama Florida.
pages.brief: South Florida and the Everglades region are shown, with Everglades National Park as a small part of the larger subtropical wilderness. Hot, wet summers and mild, dry winters are suggested, and water connects different ecosystems where mammals, reptiles, birds, and fish live.

pages.text: To the north are freshwater cypress swamps. They are named for the cypress trees that grow there. Cypress swamps cover an area bigger than the state of Rhode Island! They are home to many kinds of animals, including panthers, rabbits, turkey, and deer. Mangrove swamps are saltwater swamps. They are located at the Everglades’ southern tip. Mangrove trees, which grow there, have long roots that rise above the water. Trees with Knees Cypress trees have strange-looking growths, called knees. They grow up from the tree’s roots. Part of these knees lives above water, helping bring air to the rest of the roots. The other part lives below the water, helping anchor, or support, the whole root system.
pages.brief: Freshwater cypress swamps in the north show cypress trees and their knee growths above and below water, with panthers, rabbits, turkeys, and deer among them. Saltwater mangrove swamps at the southern tip show mangrove trees with long roots rising above the water.

pages.text: Indigenous Peoples of the Everglades The Calusa were the first Indigenous people to own and care for the Everglades region. They had a complex society, but most of them died from European diseases. The Seminole tribe was formed from Indigenous groups across Florida, Georgia, and Alabama. In 1835, the U.S. military started a war against the Seminole people. They followed their leader, Abiaka, into the swampy Everglades area. The U.S. military never conquered the Seminole people. Today, these determined people have their own government, schools, and police. They also own the Hard Rock Hotels and Casinos. Mangrove trees have long roots. They hold the trees steady as ocean tides rise and fall. The roots are also home to other living things, including algae and tiny shellfish. Fish hide in the roots to keep safe from animals that might eat them.
pages.brief: The Calusa and the Seminole, formed from groups across Florida, Georgia, and Alabama, are shown. Leader Abiaka leads Seminole people into the swampy Everglades during an 1835 war with the U.S. military. Modern Seminole government, schools, police, and hotels appear, while mangrove roots shelter algae, tiny shellfish, and hiding fish.

pages.text: Between the different swamps are sawgrass marshes. Sawgrass is a tall plant that grows in water. Each blade of grass has sharp teeth, like a saw. Alligators living in the marshes use sawgrass to build their nests.
pages.brief: Sawgrass marshes lie between the different swamps, with tall sawgrass plants growing in the water. Each blade has sharp teeth like a saw. Alligators living in the marshes use sawgrass to build their nests.

pages.text: Trees thick with leaves grow in areas called hardwood hammocks. The leaves block sunlight and shade the ground. They limit the light so much that few plants can grow. Some plants grow on the trees instead in order to reach toward sunlight. Ecosystems of the Everglades.
pages.brief: Hardwood hammocks show trees thick with leaves that block sunlight and shade the ground, limiting light so few plants can grow. Some plants grow on the trees instead, reaching toward sunlight. Around them, the different ecosystems of the Everglades are shown.

pages.text: A Park Is Born For many years, white settlers left the Everglades alone. Then, in 1903, the United States government gave 20 million acres (8,000,000 km 2 ) of land to Florida. These developers, and the U.S. government, wanted to drain the land and turn it into farms. Developers also wanted to build and sell homes there. Before long, they started drying out the land. The Everglades was slowly being destroyed. Some people wanted to protect the Everglades, including a writer named Marjory Stoneman Douglas. River of Grass In the 1940s, Stoneman Douglas wrote a book called The Everglades: River of Grass, which was a great success. It helped save the area’s natural resources by bringing attention to the park project.
pages.brief: For many years white settlers leave the Everglades alone, then in 1903 the U.S. government gives 20 million acres to Florida. Developers and the government drain land for farms and homes, slowly destroying the Everglades. Writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas writes about the Everglades in the 1940s, helping bring attention to protecting the area.

pages.text: Stoneman Douglas spent five years studying the Everglades. She wrote about making the Everglades a national park. In 1934, the United States government agreed to set aside 1.5 million acres (6,070 km 2 ) for a park. Times were hard, though, and there was no money to make it happen. Finally, in 1947, through the hard work of people like Stoneman Douglas, Everglades National Park was created.
pages.brief: Marjory Stoneman Douglas studies the Everglades for five years and writes about making it a national park. In 1934 the U.S. government agrees to set aside 1.5 million acres for a park, but there is no money. Finally, in 1947, Everglades National Park is created through hard work.

pages.text: Protecting the Park Today, the park is protected from development. However, it faces other challenges. Dozens of animal and plant species living in Everglades National Park are in danger. Their homes are at risk due to the impact of human-created climate change on weather patterns. How Fire Saves the Marshes Unlike a swamp, a marsh has no trees, which is in part due to fires. Florida has many lightning storms and these often start brush fires. The fires burn any plants or trees growing in the marsh. The fire kills young trees. It does not kill the sawgrass, however. Sawgrass roots grow deep and stay safe in a marsh’s wet, rich soil. When the fire passes, the plant sprouts new leaves.
pages.brief: Everglades National Park is protected from development but faces other challenges, with dozens of plant and animal species in danger as changing weather patterns put their homes at risk. In a marsh, lightning starts brush fires that burn young trees, but sawgrass roots stay safe in wet soil and sprout new leaves after the fire.

pages.text: The balance of life in the park is changing as well. This is because non-native species now live in Florida. These plants and animals came to Florida from other places. Some are pets that have been turned loose. Some are plants that grew from seeds people threw away. Other seeds were carried into the state by the wind. These new species create problems by eating animals and plants that native species need in order to live. Special programs have been put in place to clear the Everglades of unwanted species.
pages.brief: Non-native plants and animals now live in Florida, some from pets turned loose, some from seeds people threw away, and some carried by wind. These new species create problems by eating animals and plants that native species need. Special programs work to clear the Everglades of unwanted species.

pages.text: Into the Wild Today, many people come to the Everglades. They hike on trails through the swamps, paddle through the marshes, and camp under the hardwood hammocks. There is an amazing variety of life to see along the way.
pages.brief: Many people come to the Everglades today. They hike on trails through the swamps, paddle through the marshes, and camp under the hardwood hammocks. Along the way they see an amazing variety of life in the park.

pages.text: Everglades National Park is a special place with many unusual plants and animals. People from all over the world come to see them in their natural state. They also come to admire the natural beauty of the Everglades, a park like no other. Everglades National Park by the Numbers  1.5 million acres (607,000 ha)  Over 1 million visitors each year  More than 40 types of mammals  Over 360 types of birds  About 120 different types of trees  More than 50 unique kinds of reptiles.
pages.brief: Everglades National Park is a special place with many unusual plants and animals. People from all over the world come to see them in their natural state and admire the natural beauty of the park, a place like no other. Visitors and wildlife appear together.

books.title: Badlands National Park
books.art_why: Badlands National Park is a real modern place with living animals and current visitors, so photographs suit it.

pages.text: Badlands National Park.
pages.brief: A wide view of Badlands National Park, with bare rocky ridges and peaks rising above dry brown land under a broad sky. The open landscape shows the park's rock formations and the space around them.

pages.text: Water and wind created the Badlands. Those forces are still hard at work there today. What’s Good About the Badlands? Grasses wave in the breeze. Bison feed in the distance. A prairie dog squeaks and disappears into a hole. Then the grasslands end, and the earth opens up. Bare, rocky ridges and peaks point toward the sky. The land is dry and brown, but sometimes the Sun shines just right. Then the rocks and fields of grass display amazing colors. Badlands National Park (BNP) is a strange and amazing place.
pages.brief: A wide view of Badlands National Park: grasses wave in the breeze, bison feed in the distance, and a prairie dog disappears into a hole. The grassland ends at bare rocky ridges and peaks pointing skyward. Sunlight brings out amazing colors in the rocks and grassy fields.

pages.text: The Park Badlands National Park is located in what is South Dakota today. Different Native American groups have lived in the area for a very long time. They believe this land is special. Land of the Lakota The Lakota people have lived near Badlands National Park for more than two hundred years. They call it mako sica (mah-KOH SHEE-chah). In their language, it means “land that is bad.” Scientists also use the word badlands to describe land where soft rock has been worn away by weather.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Badlands in what is South Dakota today, with rocky ridges and grassy land. A group of Lakota people stand near the land, looking out over it. The scene suggests a place they have lived near for more than two hundred years and consider special.

pages.text: Badlands became a national park in 1978. Today, about one million people visit each year. The park is made up of three areas, but most people visit the North Unit. The other two areas are inside Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. Pine Ridge is home to the Oglala Lakota people. Part of BNP is near and around Buffalo Gap National Grassland. Together, they protect a huge space that keeps wild plants, animals, and land safe.
pages.brief: Many visitors explore the North Unit of Badlands National Park, among rocky ridges and grassland. Nearby, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation is home to the Oglala Lakota people. Buffalo Gap National Grassland stretches around part of the park, protecting wild plants, animals, and land.

pages.text: Scientists have been able to figure out the geological history of BNP through the different-colored layers of rock in the hills. Rocks and Grass Geologists are scientists who study rocks, soil, and land to learn about the history of Earth. BNP makes their job easier. The bare layers of rock show how the land formed. Each layer took millions of years to make. At different times, ash, sand, and mud settled on top of each other. Each layer turned to rock. Later, water and wind wore down the rock layers.
pages.brief: Geologists stand before bare layers of rock in a Badlands hill, studying the different bands. The layers show how ash, sand, and mud settled on top of each other over millions of years and turned to rock. Water and wind have worn down the rock layers.

pages.text: Layers of Badlands National Park The Sharps Formation includes the highest ridges and peaks in the park. Its white base is Rockyford Ash, made by ash from volcanoes. 25–30 million years ago The Brule Formation marks a time when the land was covered with grass and trees. 30–34 million years ago The Chadron (SHA-druhn) Formation is from the clay of wet marshes and swamps. Alligator fossils have been found at this level. 34–37 million years ago Yellow Mounds is made mostly of fossil remains. They formed as a great sea disappeared. 69–75 million years ago Pierre (PEER) Shale was once black mud at the bottom of that sea. It turned into a kind of rock called shale. Fossils of ancient sea creatures tell the history of this layer. How do scientists study geology? They start at the bottom. There, they usually find the oldest rocks. What story do BNP’s rock layers tell? 69–75 million years ago.
pages.brief: A close view of stacked rock layers in Badlands National Park, from dark shale at the bottom to white ash at the top. The layers show ancient sea mud, fossil-rich mounds, wet marsh clay, grassy land, and volcanic ash. Scientists start at the bottom to study the oldest rocks.

pages.text: Fossils in each layer show that the land has gone through big changes. Fossils are remains of plants and animals that have turned to rock. Fossils in the park show that the area was once like a jungle, long before humans lived there. At other times, it was covered in forests and a wide sea. Fossil Finds Many amazing fossils have been found in Badlands National Park. They include the remains of prehistoric mammals like giant rhinoceroses and three-toed horses. In 2010, a seven-year- old Junior Ranger named Kylie Ferguson discovered a fossil of a saber-toothed cat!
pages.brief: A seven-year-old Junior Ranger named Kylie Ferguson kneels on rocky ground, finding a fossil of a saber-toothed cat. Around her, the Badlands show fossils of prehistoric mammals like giant rhinoceroses and three-toed horses. The land suggests it was once a jungle, then forests, then a wide sea.

pages.text: Not all of BNP is rocky ridges and valleys. Some areas are mixed-grass prairie. A prairie is a wide, flat plain covered with grass. Few trees grow there. Two hundred years ago, prairie covered much of what is now the United States. Most of that grassland has been turned into farm fields, roads, and towns. BNP protects the largest mixed-grass prairie in any national park.
pages.brief: A wide, flat mixed-grass prairie under a broad sky, covered with waving grasses and few trees. The open plain stretches far. This protected grassland is the largest mixed-grass prairie in any national park, a small piece of the prairie that covered much of the United States two hundred years ago.

pages.text: Beasts of the Badlands Many kinds of animals make their homes in BNP. They include mammals, reptiles, birds, and insects. They must be able to live in tough weather. Winters are cold, with strong winds. Summers can be dry and hot. Storms can strike anytime of year. Visitors may spot bighorn sheep in rocky areas. Signs along dusty trails tell visitors to “Beware Rattlesnakes.” Rattlesnakes use a rattle on their tail to warn away what scares them. A rattlesnake bite can be dangerous. However, these snakes prefer to sneak away rather than bite anyone.
pages.brief: A bighorn sheep stands on rocky ground in Badlands National Park. Nearby, a rattlesnake rests on a dusty trail, its tail rattle visible. The scene shows animals living in a place with cold, windy winters, hot dry summers, and storms that can strike anytime.

pages.text: The park’s grasslands are where most wildlife is found. Big brown bison feed on grasses. Prairie dogs dig tunnels. Their towns, or groups of tunnels, may cover large areas. At night, prairie dogs may be hunted by rare black-footed ferrets. In 1987, scientists started a successful program that helped save these ferrets in BNP and other places. The grasslands are also home to swift fox and mule deer.
pages.brief: In the park's grassland, big brown bison feed on grasses. Prairie dogs dig tunnels, making towns that cover large areas. At night, a rare black-footed ferret hunts near the tunnels. A swift fox and a mule deer stand nearby in the same grassland habitat.

pages.text: More than two hundred types of birds have been seen in the park. Hawks hunt from above. Bluebirds dart after insects. Quail race through the grass. Owls make their homes in empty prairie dog tunnels. Park rangers ask visitors to stay at least 100 yards (91.5 m) from any wildlife. Keeping a safe distance protects both wildlife and people.
pages.brief: A hawk circles above the grassland while a bluebird darts after insects and a quail races through the grass. An owl sits at the opening of an empty prairie dog tunnel. A park ranger stands far from the wildlife, keeping a safe distance of at least 100 yards.

pages.text: Planning a Visit Badlands National Park is a great reason for a road trip across the rolling prairie. Visitors should be prepared, though. There are few places to eat, shop, or stay near the park. Smart hikers wear good shoes and bring plenty of water. Many visitors explore the park from their car or camper. A winding 31-mile (50 km) road crosses BNP. It has many places to take pictures of the land as the Sun shows off the park’s colors and shadows.
pages.brief: A winding road crosses the rolling prairie and rocky Badlands. A car and a camper travel along it, stopping at a place where visitors take pictures of the land as the Sun shows colors and shadows. Nearby, smart hikers wear good shoes and carry plenty of water.

pages.text: Badlands National Park offers a journey back in time. It is easy to imagine people on horseback riding through the tall grass. Rocky ridges and valleys tell the history of the park’s land. Wildlife live as they have for centuries. The Badlands of South Dakota are as beautiful as they are bad.
pages.brief: People on horseback ride through tall grass near rocky ridges and valleys in the Badlands of South Dakota. Wildlife live nearby as they have for centuries. The wide landscape shows the park's long history, looking as beautiful as it is bad.

books.title: Salmon: A Link in the Food Chain
books.art_why: Real salmon, other animals, rivers, estuaries, and oceans can be photographed.

pages.text: A Chain of Life Imagine a chain. Each link is connected to the next. One link cannot be broken without affecting the other links in the chain. Salmon are links in many different food chains. As salmon go through the stages of their life, they eat and are eaten by different living things.
pages.brief: A chain of connected links is shown, and salmon at different life stages appear as links; each link touches the next, and the salmon are connected to other living things as they eat and are eaten.

pages.text: Let’s look at the food chain for an adult salmon. It begins with plankton, tiny living organisms. Plankton are eaten by small fish such as herring. Herring are then eaten by salmon. A salmon may be eaten by a human, a bear, a killer whale, a seal, or an eagle. Harming one living thing in a food chain harms other living things in the chain.
pages.brief: In an ocean-and-river scene, tiny plankton float in the water; small herring swim near them; a large adult salmon swims among the herring. Around the water, on the shore and in the air, a human, a bear, a killer whale, a seal and an eagle are shown as animals that may eat the salmon.

pages.text: Salmon are travelers. They start their lives in streams or rivers and then migrate far into the ocean. Finally, they return to the very same place to spawn, or reproduce. Salmon are transformers. They change shape and color many times in their life. In this book, you will learn about the salmon life cycle and the ways they are interconnected with other animals and with their environment.
pages.brief: A salmon is shown in a stream or river, then far out in the ocean, then back at the same river place to spawn. Along the way its body is shown changing shape and color many times, illustrating that salmon are travelers and transformers.

pages.text: Eggs Salmon begin as tiny eggs laid in the gravel of a riverbed or streambed. Salmon need cold, clean water in order to lay and fertilize eggs. If the temperature is too warm, the salmon may die before the eggs are laid. Salmon absorb oxygen from the water. If the water is polluted, making it low in oxygen, salmon cannot breathe and will die. Water is a salmon’s environment. If it is harmed, salmon and the eggs they lay will be, too.
pages.brief: Tiny salmon eggs lie in the gravel of a cold, clean riverbed or streambed. Clear water flows around them, carrying oxygen. The scene shows the eggs in the water environment, with the riverbed gravel and water conditions that salmon need for laying and fertilizing eggs and for breathing.

pages.text: Alevins and Fry The eggs hatch after about two weeks. The tiny salmon that emerge, called alevins (AL-uh-vins), have their food attached to their bodies in a sac. Once the sac is empty, the alevins develop stripes and are called fry.
pages.brief: After about two weeks, tiny alevins emerge from eggs in the riverbed gravel. Each alevin has a food sac attached to its body. One alevin is shown with an empty sac, its body developing stripes, becoming a fry.

pages.text: Fry eat plankton. If there are not enough plankton, the fry will starve. Plankton also need to live in clean, cool water. Plankton are a link in the food chain, and if it is disturbed, the fry will be, too.
pages.brief: Small striped fry swim in clean, cool water and eat tiny plankton drifting around them. The water is clear and cool. The fry and plankton are shown together as links in a food chain, with the fry feeding on the plankton in the water.

pages.text: Smolts The amazing journey begins as fry change from brown to shiny silver and transform into smolts, the next stage in their life cycle. Smolts eat insects. If there are not enough insects to eat, the smolts will not have enough energy to complete their migration to the sea. Insects are links in the food chain. If they are disturbed, the salmon will be, too.
pages.brief: A brown fry changes into a shiny silver smolt in the river. The smolt swims near insects and eats them, gaining energy for its migration to the sea. The insects and the smolt are shown as connected links in the food chain.

pages.text: The smolts journey downstream to an area between the river and the ocean called an estuary. An estuary is where the fresh water and salt water combine to form brackish water. Smolts need the perfect estuary to prepare their bodies for the ocean and its salty water. If the estuary doesn’t have just the right balance of fresh water and salt water, the smolts cannot make the changes they need to survive in the sea.
pages.brief: Smolts swim downstream to an estuary where river fresh water and ocean salt water combine into brackish water. The estuary lies between the river and the ocean. The smolts are shown in this mixing water, preparing their bodies for the salty ocean.

pages.text: Some estuaries have become polluted with chemicals. The fish absorb those chemicals. This can harm or kill the fish. If the smolt absorbs pollution into its body and then a bird eats the smolt, the bird becomes poisoned. Smolts are part of the food chain. If they are disturbed, the birds will be, too. Already we can see that water, fish, plankton, insects, and birds are all connected.
pages.brief: In a polluted estuary, chemicals are shown in the water. A smolt absorbs the chemicals into its body. A bird eats the smolt and becomes poisoned. Nearby, water, fish, plankton, insects and birds are shown connected in the same food chain.

pages.text: Do You Know? Some scientists think that salmon memorize the scent of their own river and smell their way home. Adults In the estuary, the smolts will develop into adult salmon. Then they scatter into the open ocean. The adult salmon live and feed on smaller fish in the ocean for one to seven years, traveling thousands of miles. When the time comes to reproduce, the salmon make the long swim back to the same river where they were hatched. These salmon will become spawners.
pages.brief: Adult salmon scatter into the open ocean from the estuary and feed on smaller fish for one to seven years, traveling thousands of miles. A salmon is shown smelling its way back to the scent of its own river. When ready to reproduce, it swims back to the same river where it hatched.

pages.text: Spawners As adult salmon return to fresh water, they lose their shiny, silvery color. The males change to bright red and green, and grow a hooked nose and large teeth. The females turn a dull red. The males and females struggle against powerful currents as they swim upstream. Spawners do not eat during their voyage. Instead, they burn the fat they have stored from feeding in the ocean.
pages.brief: Spawners swim upstream against powerful currents in fresh water. The males are bright red and green with a hooked nose and large teeth; the females are dull red. Their shiny silver color is gone. They do not eat on the voyage and burn fat stored from ocean feeding.

pages.text: The trip upstream is dangerous because spawners are the favorite food of bears and eagles. Bears can be spotted fishing for salmon on the banks of rivers and estuaries. Bears need a great deal of body fat to make it through the winter. Salmon skin is loaded with fat. If there are many salmon, the bears will eat only the nutritious skin and leave the rest.
pages.brief: On the banks of a river and estuary, bears fish for spawners in the water. A bear eats only the nutritious skin of a salmon and leaves the rest, because bears need a great deal of body fat to make it through winter. Eagles are also nearby.

pages.text: Eagles also love salmon. They catch their own, or they eat what the bears have left. Humans also eat salmon. Salmon are a link in the food chain, and if they are disturbed, the bears, eagles, and humans will be, too.
pages.brief: An eagle catches its own salmon or eats what the bears have left. Nearby, humans eat salmon. The eagle, humans, bears and salmon are shown together as links in a food chain, with salmon as food for bears, eagles and humans.

pages.text: Humans have constructed dams in many rivers. These prevent spawners from returning home to spawn. Fewer eggs mean fewer new salmon and less food for birds, bears, and humans. Water is part of the spawners’ environment. If it is disturbed, the salmon, bears, birds, and humans will be, too.
pages.brief: A dam built by humans blocks a river. Spawners gather below it, unable to return home to spawn. In the river and around it, birds, bears and humans are shown as part of the food chain that receives less food when fewer new salmon are produced.

pages.text: Once the spawners make it home, the females lay eggs and the males fertilize them. The salmon die about a week later. But they do not go to waste. Birds, bears, and other animals eat their bodies. Nutrients from the spawners’ flesh and bones also provide food for plankton.
pages.brief: At home in the river, a female spawner lays eggs and a male fertilizes them. About a week later the salmon die. Birds, bears and other animals eat their bodies. Nutrients from the spawners’ flesh and bones are shown feeding plankton in the water.

pages.text: Conclusion Salmon are amazing. They begin their lives in a riverbed or streambed, travel to an ocean, and return to the place they were born. Their bodies transform at each stage of their journey. Salmon are important links in many food chains. These food chains change during different parts of a salmon’s life. What happens to salmon affects what happens to other living things in these food chains. Some types of salmon grow very large—up to 135 pounds, or about 61 kg.
pages.brief: A salmon is shown at each stage: beginning in a riverbed or streambed, traveling to an ocean, and returning to the place it was born. Its body transforms along the way. A very large salmon is shown, up to 135 pounds or about 61 kg, as an important link in food chains.

books.title: The Yanomami: Deep in the Amazon
books.art_why: The book shows real rainforest places, wildlife, and Yanomami people who exist today.

pages.text: The Yanomami: Deep in the Amazon.
pages.brief: A dense Amazon rainforest scene with tall green trees, vines, and a winding river, suggesting a remote place deep in the forest. The view introduces the Yanomami and their rainforest home, with sunlight filtering through the canopy onto broad leaves and quiet water.

pages.text: The Amazon The planet’s oldest living ecosystems are rainforests. Rainforests exist on every continent except Antarctica and have been around for more than seventy million years! The largest rainforest on Earth is the Amazon rainforest in South America. Rainforests like the Amazon are important because they are one of the most diverse habitats on Earth. They are home to people, including Indigenous tribes such as the Yanomami (yah-noh-MAH-mee). They are also home to 80% of the world’s plant and animal species. Without the essential habitats rainforests offer, the Earth could face the decline or extinction of much of its wildlife. Rainforests also help clean the Earth’s air and water and regulate its climate. They are sometimes called natural air filters because rainforest trees can remove pollution from the air and release clean oxygen. Rainforests provide a similar filtering effect to Earth’s waterways. Without rainforests, life on Earth would not be the same.
pages.brief: An aerial view of the vast Amazon rainforest in South America, with a wide river winding through dense green canopy. Small figures of Indigenous Yanomami people stand near the trees, showing that this diverse habitat is home to people as well as 80 percent of the world’s plant and animal species.

pages.text: Living for Today and Tomorrow The people of the Yanomami tribe, one of the world’s oldest cultures, call the Amazon rainforest home. Indigenous tribes like the Yanomami have lived in the Amazon for more than five thousand years. The Yanomami live in what is known today as Brazil and Venezuela, although the Yanomami lived there long before those countries ever existed. The Yanomami have collected thousands of years of knowledge about the Amazon rainforest. Their lifestyle is dependent on living in harmony with the rainforest’s many species of plants and animals. Because the Yanomami lifestyle relies on the rainforest, they are careful to never overuse resources or harm the environment. Yanomami Territory.
pages.brief: A Yanomami community in the Amazon rainforest, located in what is today Brazil and Venezuela. People move among trees and plants, showing a culture more than five thousand years old that lives in harmony with the rainforest’s species and carefully avoids overusing resources.

pages.text: The Yanomami live in a way that is sustainable, which means the way they live today is designed to leave a healthy rainforest for tomorrow. They avoid cutting down more trees, picking more fruit, and hunting more animals than they need to survive. They live this way in hopes that their children and grandchildren will still have the trees, fruit, and animals they need—and that the rainforest’s ecosystem will remain healthy. Rainforests and the Dangers of Deforestation As rainforests shrink, the quality of Earth’s air and water are affected. So are the habitats of hundreds of plant and animal species. Yet, deforestation, or the removal of trees, continues to be problematic for the Amazon and other rainforests.
pages.brief: A Yanomami family gathers only a few fruits and cuts only the trees they need, leaving most of the rainforest standing. Nearby, a cleared patch shows deforestation, with fallen trees and open ground, as a reminder of the harm when too many trees are removed from the Amazon.

pages.text: Life in the Rainforest For thousands of years, the Amazon rainforest has given the Yanomami all they need to survive. They have not had to rely on trade with other nations for the goods they require. Like many other Indigenous people of South America, the Yanomami believe the spiritual world is very important. They use knowledge of local plants and animals to get closer to this world. Beyond that, they use the forest to meet their daily needs, including shelter, food, and clothing. Do You Know? Yanomami can be spelled in different ways: Yanoama, Yanomama, and Yanomamo.
pages.brief: Yanomami people stand in a lush rainforest clearing, surrounded by local plants and animals. They use the forest for shelter, food, and clothing while honoring a spiritual world they believe is important. The scene shows their long reliance on the Amazon rather than trade with other nations.

pages.text: Yanos and Community The Yanomami live in big, circular huts called yanos. They build them with wooden poles, vines, and thatched leaves. Viewing a yano from above, it would look like a big circle with a hole cut out in the middle. The center of the circle, open to the sky, is where adults meet and children play. An entire Yanomami village often lives in one yano, with many families sharing the same roof. Instead of living in separate rooms, each family has its own area where family members eat and sleep. Each family has its own fire pit for cooking, and each person has their own hammock for sleep.
pages.brief: A large circular Yanomami yano made of wooden poles, vines, and thatched leaves stands in the rainforest. Seen from above, it forms a ring around an open center under the sky. Inside, several families have their own areas with fire pits and hammocks, sharing one roof.

pages.text: Gathering and Gardening The Yanomami know the rainforest well. They know which herbs to use for different illnesses; they know which plants are edible and which are poisonous. They gather wild foods such as fruit, nuts, roots, and insects. They also plant gardens in the rainforest. First they cut and burn the trees on small sections of land, then plant sugar cane, plantains, sweet potatoes, manioc, and more. To avoid harming the land, the Yanomami move their garden every few years and allow the old garden to grow back into rainforest. When the Yanomami do not have enough food from gathering and gardening, they set out on a wayumi. A wayumi is a trek through the rainforest during which the entire village travels for days or weeks while searching for food. On wayumis, the Yanomami eat roots, make hammocks out of bark, and sleep under leaves to keep dry.
pages.brief: Yanomami people work in a small rainforest garden, planting sugar cane, plantains, sweet potatoes, and manioc after cutting and burning a small patch. Others gather wild fruit, nuts, roots, and insects nearby. The scene shows their knowledge of edible and poisonous plants and their care to let old gardens grow back.

pages.text: Hunting and Fishing Yanomami hunters hunt using longbows and wooden arrows with bird feathers attached to help them fly straight. Sometimes they dip their arrowheads in poison. Hunters walk barefoot through the rainforest looking for anteaters, tapirs, and other animals. When hunters kill animals, they share the meat with the entire village. The Yanomami use a variety of methods to catch fish. Some shoot arrows at fish in the river, while others skim baskets through the water. The Yanomami also know how to fish with the poisonous ayori-toto vine. They cut the vine and slide it through the water, and the poison drips into the water stunning nearby fish. The fish then float to the surface, and the Yanomami scoop them up.
pages.brief: A Yanomami hunter walks barefoot through the rainforest with a longbow and feathered wooden arrows, searching for anteaters, tapirs, and other animals. Near a river, others fish with bows and baskets or use the poisonous ayori-toto vine to stun fish. Hunted meat is shared with the whole village.

pages.text: Yanomami Fashion The clothing choices people make often depend on where they live, how they live, and what materials are available. The Yanomami get everything they need from the rainforest— and use it with the rainforest’s conditions in mind. The rainforest is often hot and rainy, so the Yanomami dress lightly to stay cool and mobile. Men often wear loincloths, women often wear fringed aprons, and children tend to wear little or no clothing for their own comfort in the heat. The Yanomami often paint their bodies with different colors. They use red dyes from seeds, purple dyes from palm fruit, and black powder from charcoal. Many of their designs involve patterns with dots and lines.
pages.brief: Yanomami men, women, and children stand in the hot, rainy rainforest wearing light clothing: loincloths, fringed aprons, and little or nothing for the children. Adults paint their bodies with red seed dyes, purple palm-fruit dyes, and black charcoal powder, creating patterns of dots and lines.

pages.text: Some Yanomami tattoo rather than paint their markings on, and their tattoos have a variety of different cultural purposes. Tattoos can serve as a link to the spiritual world. They can also demonstrate a person’s accomplishments or mark their transition into adulthood. Some Yanomami people pierce their noses, lips, and ears. They use small wooden sticks as nose and lip rings and bird feathers for earrings. They also wear other jewelry made from the rainforest, such as necklaces of seeds and armbands of fragrant leaves. Sometimes they crown their heads with small, white hawk feathers.
pages.brief: A Yanomami man and woman display body tattoos and piercings, with small wooden sticks in noses and lips and bird-feather earrings. They wear seed necklaces and fragrant-leaf armbands, and one person has a crown of small white hawk feathers. Their markings show spiritual links, personal accomplishments, and the transition into adulthood.

pages.text: Yanomami Land Today About 20,000 Yanomami remain in the Amazon today. They live similar to the way their ancestors did, still hunting, gathering food, sleeping under yanos, and fashioning their clothing from materials in the rainforest. But in the last fifty years, more outsiders have arrived—and they do not share the Yanomami’s knowledge of or respect for the rainforest. These outsiders travel by motorized boats, trucks, and airplanes, and they come looking to benefit from the fertile and mineral-rich lands. They mine, hunt, fish, and cut down trees in ways that are not sustainable. Unlike the Yanomami, they are not careful to keep the rainforest healthy. In the 1970s, the number of outsiders coming to the rainforest increased. Many of the outsiders were garimpeiros, a Portuguese word for “wildcat gold miners.” The garimpeiros entered Yanomami land hoping to strike it rich; they cared more about finding gold than the harm they could do to the rainforest.
pages.brief: A Yanomami family stands near a traditional yano while outsiders arrive in motorized boats, trucks, and a small airplane. The newcomers carry mining tools and cut trees, hunting and fishing unsustainably. The scene shows the growing pressure on about 20,000 Yanomami and their land from gold miners and others since the 1970s.

pages.text: Gold-mining is one of the largest threats to the Yanomami and the rainforest. Unfortunately, the appeal of getting rich has increased illegal mining. The consequences of gold-mining have devastated the rainforest in many ways, not only through the loss of trees, but also through pollution caused by toxic chemicals entering major waterways and the soil. Between the effects of the outsiders and the destructive nature of forest fires caused by global warming, life for the Yanomami and the Amazon rainforest itself is in great danger. If the rainforest continues to be destroyed, the whole world will suffer alongside the Yanomami, since the rainforest helps maintain a healthy global climate. The Yanomami must deal with outsiders and the problems they bring, including diseases and the destruction and pollution of the forest that supports the Yanomami’s lifestyle.
pages.brief: An illegal gold-mining camp beside a rainforest river shows torn earth, fallen trees, and muddy water. Toxic chemicals seep into waterways and soil while smoke from forest fires rises in the distance. The scene shows how mining, pollution, disease, and climate-driven fires threaten the Yanomami and the Amazon rainforest that supports their way of life.

pages.text: Conclusion The Yanomami culture is rich with centuries of knowledge about the Amazon rainforest and the discipline and skills needed to live sustainably. Although many people have never interacted directly with the Yanomami, the problems they are facing have captured attention worldwide. The Yanomami have been depicted in books, magazines, movies, and art. Many who study their culture want to help others learn to prevent further negative impacts on the Yanomami and the Amazon rainforest. The Amazon rainforest is important to everyone on Earth. It produces a lot of the world’s oxygen, affects the world’s climate, supports a large variety of plant and animal life, and of course—is home to the Yanomami people.
pages.brief: A Yanomami person stands in the rainforest beside a display of books, magazines, and artwork that depict Yanomami culture. The wide Amazon forest behind them supports varied plant and animal life and helps produce oxygen and regulate climate. The scene suggests worldwide attention and a desire to protect their home.

books.title: Butterflies and Moths
books.art_why: Real butterflies, moths, gardens and nature scenes can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Butterflies and moths can be beautiful to watch. People plant gardens to attract butterflies. Butterflies at zoos and city gardens draw large crowds. However, no one builds a garden to attract moths. Many people think of moths as pests. So, how are butterflies and moths the same, and how are they different? What makes a butterfly a butterfly? What makes a moth a moth? To answer these questions, we need to learn about their body parts, life cycle, and behavior. Do You Know? The largest butterfly in the world is the Queen Alexandra’s birdwing. From wingtip to wingtip it can be as wide as 30 cm (12 in). It is found in Papua New Guinea.
pages.brief: Visitors stand along a bright flower garden at a zoo or city garden, watching butterflies flutter among plants. Nearby, a huge Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly is shown with wide wings, suggesting its record size in Papua New Guinea.

pages.text: What Are Butterflies and Moths? Butterflies and moths are insects. Like all insect species, they are invertebrates, which means they have no backbone. Instead, they have a hard skin, called an exoskeleton, that protects their soft insides. They also have six legs, a body divided into three parts, two antennae, and two compound eyes. Their wings are covered with scales, which are like fine, flat hairs. These scales protect the wings from getting too wet and help them hold in heat. Butterflies cannot fly if they are too cold. They often sit in the sun to warm up before flying. wings body scales antenna eye tube-like mouth legs.
pages.brief: A close-up photo shows a butterfly resting on a leaf in sunlight, its six legs, three body parts, two antennae, compound eyes and scaled wings visible. Another view shows the hard outer skin and tube-like mouth as it warms up.

pages.text: Butterflies and moths have many of the same body parts, so it is easy to see why people have trouble telling them apart. antenna head thorax abdomen wings moth butterfly • Compound eyes made up of many smaller eyes allowing them to see all around them Head • Antennae to smell and to sense movement • Mouth is a long tube for sucking nectar Do You Know? More than 165,000 kinds, or species, of butterflies and moths exist. Most of these are moths. It is believed that another 100,000 species exist that have not been studied or identified. • Two pairs of wings • Three pairs of legs Thorax • Breathing holes • Digestive organs • Reproductive organs Abdomen • Breathing holes.
pages.brief: A side-by-side photo shows a moth and a butterfly on a branch, with antennae, head, thorax, abdomen, two pairs of wings and legs. A close view shows their compound eyes and long tube mouths for sucking nectar.

pages.text: However, butterflies and moths are also different from each other in many ways. The next time you find a butterfly or moth, use this chart to help you tell which kind of insect you have found. Butterflies Moths Most are active at night. Most are active during the day. Most are dull in color. Most are brightly colored. “Fat, furry” body Skinny body without “fur” Plain or feathery antennae Most have antennae with knobs. Most rest with their wings spread out flat at the sides of their body. Most rest with their wings above their body. Tiny hook or bristle that links each forewing and hindwing while in flight Enlarged lobe on each hind wing that provides overlap.
pages.brief: A side-by-side nature photo shows a butterfly and a moth on plants. The butterfly has a slender body, bright wings and knobbed antennae held above its back; the moth has a fat, furry body, dull wings and feathery antennae spread flat.

pages.text: Life Cycle After a pair of male and female butterflies or moths mate, the female lays her eggs. She lays them on or near leaves, twigs, or flowers so that her young will have something to eat when they hatch. Lobster moth egg White butterfly eggs.
pages.brief: A close-up photo shows a female butterfly or moth laying tiny eggs on a leaf, twig, or flower in a garden. Nearby, lobster moth eggs and white butterfly eggs rest in small clusters on plant surfaces.

pages.text: When eggs hatch, caterpillars come out. This begins the larval stage of the butterfly and moth life cycle. Caterpillars have chewing mouth parts and can eat 27,000 times their body weight during their lifetime. Their egg case is often their first meal, followed by the leaf or flower they’re on, and then the rest of the plant. A caterpillar’s job is to eat and grow. As it grows, its skin becomes tight and breaks away. A new skin grows in its place to allow the caterpillar to get bigger. This is called molting. A caterpillar molts four or five times during its life. The caterpillar is fully grown after about two weeks.
pages.brief: A caterpillar emerges from an egg case on a leaf and begins eating the leaf and flower around it. Another view shows its tight old skin splitting away as a new skin grows, while it feeds and grows bigger on the plant.

pages.text: The life of caterpillars is filled with danger. They are food for many larger animals, such as lizards, birds, bats, and small mammals. Caterpillars have many interesting ways to protect themselves from being eaten. Some caterpillars have spines and other hairs that make them taste bad to predators. Others have colors or patterns on their bodies that make them appear more dangerous than they are. Caterpillars also can be masters at hiding, blending in with their background, or staying still until night comes, or until the danger goes away. The swallowtail butterfly caterpillar has red horns that release a strong odor to keep away predators. Many caterpillars feed on plants that make them taste bad to birds and other enemies. These caterpillars often are brightly colored to warn others: Do not eat me! Owl butterfly caterpillar.
pages.brief: A swallowtail butterfly caterpillar shows red horns that release a strong odor. Nearby, an owl butterfly caterpillar blends into leaves, while other caterpillars display bright colors, spines or hairs to warn predators such as lizards, birds, bats and small mammals.

pages.text: Do You Know? The pupa cannot move to escape predators. Many butterfly chrysalises are well hidden by looking like a dead leaf or piece of bark. Some chrysalises are poisonous and are brightly colored to tell predators that they are not good to eat. When a caterpillar is fully grown, it enters the pupal stage. In this stage, a caterpillar slowly changes into an adult. It appears dead from the outside, but amazing changes are happening inside. The caterpillars of most butterflies enter this stage by sticking their back end onto a twig, leaf, or other object. The last molt leaves a soft pupal skin that hardens into a case called a chrysalis. The caterpillars of many moths go through the pupal stage underground or on the ground. Others spin a cocoon to protect themselves.
pages.brief: A fully grown caterpillar sticks its rear end to a twig and becomes a hard chrysalis that looks like a dead leaf or bark. Another photo shows a moth caterpillar underground or spinning a cocoon around itself on the ground.

pages.text: Just a few hours after the pupal stage begins, different mouth parts, legs, new muscles, and tiny wings begin to form. The change from pupa to adult can take a few weeks. The entire change from egg to larva to pupa, and then to adult, is called metamorphosis. When the adult is fully formed, it breaks out of the case. Its wings, which are damp and crumpled, must expand, dry, and harden before the insect can fly. When the butterfly or moth comes out of its chrysalis, it is adult in size and will not grow any more. Do You Know? For most butterflies and moths, life is short! Adults live for two weeks to two months, except for the monarch, which can live from nine to twelve months.
pages.brief: Inside a clear pupal case, new mouth parts, legs, muscles and tiny wings form. An adult butterfly or moth breaks out, its damp crumpled wings spreading and drying in the air before it can fly, already adult-sized and no longer growing.

pages.text: Do You Know? Lantana and butterfly bush are great plants for attracting beautiful butterflies to your garden. If you want to attract moths at night, try smearing mashed banana and honey on a tree trunk. Keep watch with a flashlight. Life as an Adult Adult butterflies and moths come in many shapes, sizes, and colors. Many butterflies are brightly colored, but others are white or light colored. While many moths have dull colors, some, such as the luna moth, have amazing colors or patterns. Adult butterflies and moths have many enemies. They need to be as careful as caterpillars not to get eaten. Even though adult butterflies and moths can fly, many animals that hunt them—such as birds and bats—can fly, too.
pages.brief: Adult butterflies and moths of many shapes and colors fly among flowers in a garden. A butterfly bush and lantana blossoms attract butterflies by day; at night, mashed banana and honey smeared on a tree trunk draws moths while a flashlight beam watches them.

pages.text: Adult butterflies and moths, like caterpillars, have many ways to hide to stay safe from predators. Some have patterns on their wings that help them to blend in with nature. Many patterns look exactly like leaves or flowers. Other butterflies and moths have bright patterns on their wings, such as spots that look like eyes, to scare away enemies. Some, such as the monarch butterfly, are brightly colored to warn predators that they taste bad. SPOTLIGHT ON: Buckeye Butterfly Wingspan: 4.2 to 7 cm (1.7– 2.8 in) Range: North America, from southern Canada to southern Mexico Appearance: The wings of the buckeye butterfly have large eyespots of black, blue, and yellow. The eyespots look like the eyes of a large animal. A predator may be scared when the buckeye shakes its wings and flashes its eyespots. This may give the butterfly an extra second or two to fly away before being eaten.
pages.brief: A buckeye butterfly rests on a plant, its brown wings marked with large black, blue and yellow eyespots. The butterfly shakes its wings and flashes the spots toward a nearby predator, looking like the eyes of a large animal before it flies away.

pages.text: SPOTLIGHT ON: Luna Moth Wingspan: 7.5 to 11.3 cm (3– 4.4 in) Range: Eastern and plains areas of United States and Canada Appearance: The luna moth has beautiful pastel green wings with reddish-brown edges. The unusual shape of its hind wings helps it to hide among leaves when it is resting. This is one of a few moths that never eat as an adult. It eats enough to last a lifetime while it is a caterpillar. It spends its adult life seeking a mate and laying eggs. Most adult butterflies and moths feed on nectar, a sweet liquid from flowers. They suck up nectar using their mouth parts, which look like a hollow tube and work like a straw that curls up when not in use. Butterflies and moths do not have jaws or teeth, and they do not eat solid food.
pages.brief: A pale green luna moth with reddish-brown wing edges rests among leaves, its hind wings shaped to hide it. Nearby, an adult butterfly or moth uncurls a hollow tube mouth to suck nectar from a flower, taking only liquid food.

pages.text: Butterflies have a good sense of sight, but a poor sense of smell. The flowers they eat from are brightly colored. Flowers often grow in groups that provide butterflies with a place to land. Butterflies often walk around flower groups, sucking nectar from each blossom with their mouth parts. Because most moths are active at night, most of the flowers they eat from are light colored to be seen in moonlight. These flowers often give off a sweet smell to attract them. Because moths often hover rather than land, the flowers’ petals are shaped to allow for easy eating. Butterflies and moths have sense organs in their antennae, mouth parts, legs, feet, and other parts of their bodies. These sense organs help them find food, mates, and plants on which to lay eggs.
pages.brief: Butterflies visit brightly colored flowers growing in groups, walking over blossoms and sucking nectar. At night, light-colored, sweet-smelling flowers attract hovering moths. Close views show sense organs on antennae, mouth parts, legs and feet helping them find food and mates.

pages.text: PACIFIC OCEAN Some butterflies and moths that live in cold places migrate to warmer places before winter begins. The best known butterfly that migrates is the monarch butterfly. Monarchs in North America begin their long journey south when it begins to cool off in late summer or fall. Monarchs living west of the Rocky Mountains fly to several places on the California coast. Monarchs living east of the Rockies fly as far as 4,800 kilometers (2,982 mi) to Mexico. When they reach warmer places, millions of them rest in trees through the winter. In spring, they migrate north again in search of plants on which to lay their eggs. No one knows how monarchs find their way.
pages.brief: Millions of monarch butterflies cluster on trees in warm places after flying south for winter. Some travel from North America to California or Mexico; in spring they fly north again, searching for plants where they can lay eggs.

pages.text: Conclusion Over the years, people have collected butterflies and moths for scientific study and as a hobby. Scientists and others have learned a great deal about these insects from collections. However, millions of these beautiful insects have lost their lives because of collectors. Watching butterflies and moths while they are alive is much kinder and also more interesting. You can learn a great deal about their similarities and differences just by watching them fly and feed. Take pictures of them or catch them in a net for a closer look (don’t touch!) and then let them go. View photos of your favorite species on the Internet or in a book. Build or visit a butterfly garden and keep a journal to record their activities. Do You Know? Do not touch butterflies or moths. The oils on human hands can hurt their wings. No matter how gentle you try to be, you are likely to hurt them by breaking a piece of wing or rubbing off some scales. However you choose to enjoy butterflies and moths, remember that they are among nature’s most amazing insects.
pages.brief: People watch living butterflies and moths in a garden, taking photos or gently catching one in a net for a closer look before release. A journal records their activities, and a person views species photos on the Internet or in a book.
